papers.title: Reject and Report: Forgery-Evident Undetectable Watermarks for Generative Image Models
papers.abstract: Provenance schemes such as those based on content watermarks let images from a generative model be traced back to it. A practical watermarking scheme must be accurate at a low false-positive rate (FPR), robust under content-preserving processing, and undetectable. In addition, it must resist forgery; otherwise, even from a single watermarked image and a surrogate model, an adversary can imprint the watermark onto an arbitrary image or regenerate new content that carries it, falsely attributing harmful content to a model or making authentic photographs appear AI-generated. We argue that a watermarking scheme should not only reject forgeries but also report them: a forgery rejected as unwatermarked leaves no trace of the attempt. State-of-the-art forgery-resilient undetectable watermarking schemes, such as SemBind, fall short on both counts. External anomaly detectors that do report forgeries either miss most of them or falsely flag genuine images after common processing. We propose Tripwire-WM, the first forgery-evident framework for undetectable watermarks. It commits the semantics of the generated image to the magnitudes of the initial latent noise, which the sign-based watermarks leave unused, through a distribution-preserving embedding; a forged image carries a valid watermark but with a commitment that does not match its content, so the detector both rejects it and reports it as forged. Built on the pseudorandom code (PRC) watermark and Gaussian Shading++, Tripwire-WM provably preserves their undetectability. On MS-COCO, with the owner's own model as the surrogate, it accepts no imprinting forgery, compared with up to 55.0% for SemBind, and reports all of them as forged; it also accepts at most 1.8% of reprompting forgeries, against up to 46.2% for SemBind. Meanwhile, it accepts at least 99% of genuine watermarked images at 10^{-6} FPR and matches the robustness of the base schemes.
papers.authors: Yihan Wang, Haochen Sun, Xi He, Yaoliang Yu, N. Asokan

papers.title: Correctable Enrollment and One-Transaction Seed Proofs for Ethereum's Post-Quantum Transition
papers.abstract: A quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can extract the private key of every Ethereum account whose public key is published, and accounts exposed by their own transactions hold 54.6% of execution-layer ETH. As the first such machine may stay secret, a migration cannot wait for visible thefts, and once keys are extractable, legacy signatures no longer tell owners from attackers. We design a migration in which owners enroll post-quantum keys cheaply with their existing signatures before ECDSA is retired at a scheduled time, while a zero-knowledge proof of the wallet's BIP-39 seed can correct any such enrollment until a common deadline afterward; an account nobody enrolled stays frozen and recoverable by seed proof without a deadline. Each proof binds the new key, a nonce and a fee cap, so neither a paying sponsor nor a reordering block builder can redirect or replay it. Validators switch to hash-based keys first, at a finalized checkpoint and under a stated bound on the attacker's voting power. We prove the account guarantees under explicit assumptions, model-check the rules, and implement the design in go-ethereum and a Lean consensus client. A three-layer recursive hash-based STARK yields a seed proof of about 190 KB that fits one transaction, verifies in 38 ms and takes a median of 111 s to generate on a laptop; four proofs aggregate into one. In a ten-node simulation with mainnet-derived accounts and fee demand, block space rather than proving sets the duration: the 4.45 million accounts with at least 0.1 ETH would migrate in 29.4 days if all enroll before ECDSA is retired and in 235 days if all recover after it in batches of four. In a mass enrollment, an enrollment waits a median of 19.1 minutes in the public mempool, longer than published estimates for a fast quantum computer to extract its key, so owners with a seed and an unexposed key should migrate by seed proof.
papers.authors: Xin Jin, Maximillian Liao, Handong Chen, Yi Nancy Li, Junyu Liu

papers.title: GPU-Accelerated Secure Inference for Drug--Target Interaction Prediction
papers.abstract: Deep learning models that predict drug--target interactions (DTI) can speed up drug discovery, but the candidate drugs they score are valuable intellectual property that their owners cannot reveal. Secure multiparty computation (MPC) lets two servers compute a prediction on a secret-shared drug, without either server learning the drug. However, secure inference of deep models is slow. Non-linear operations require communication between the servers, and MPC arithmetic does not map naturally to GPUs. In this paper, we present our solution to Track~III of the iDASH 2026 privacy and security competition, which asked for fast two-party secure DTI inference on GPUs. Our solution is built on the co-design of MPC-friendly models and MPC protocols. On the model side, we design SlimDTA, a DTI model that reduces the operations on the secret drug, and in particular the non-linear operations that require communication. On the protocol side, we build a GPU framework that evaluates the linear layers with additive secret sharing and the non-linear layers with function secret sharing, including a custom CUDA kernel for the comparisons. Our solution won first place in the competition, at under 10,ms per prediction on average, and its secure predictions match the plaintext model to within 0.02%.
papers.authors: Sikha Pentyala, Steven Golob, Daniil Filienko, Ming-Chun Kao, Martine De Cock

papers.title: Classical Oracle Separation of QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy and Quantum Cryptography Even When P = QCMA
papers.abstract: Remark: This work is in submission at STOC'27 and thus the full manuscript has been publicly posted on the conference website since November 3rd, 2026. Inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem recently introduced by Cakan (arXiV, 2026) to separate $\mathsf{QMA}$ from $\mathsf{QCIP}$, we introduce a new problem called Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise ($\mathsf{CHN}$) and prove that, in the query complexity model, it is in $\mathsf{QMA}$ but hard for the $\mathsf{QCMA}$ hierarchy $\mathsf{QCMAH} = \bigcup_{d\geq1}\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathsf{QCMA}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{QCMA}}}}$, the classical-witness quantum-verifier analogue of $\mathsf{PH}=\bigcup_{d\ge1}\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{NP}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{NP}}}}$. Using this problem, we show that there exists a classical oracle ${O}$ such that $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O} =\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O} \subset \mathsf{QMA}^{O} \text{ but } \mathsf{QMA}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O},$ thus showing that quantum state or quantum proof advantage could exist even if classical computers can efficiently solve any problem that can be quantumly verified with a classical proof. Further, using our problem, we show that various quantum cryptographic primitives can exist even when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{QCMA}$ and thus neither quantum-computable one-way functions nor (verifiable) quantum computational advantage exist. In particular, relative to a classical oracle ${O}$ with $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O}$, there exist pseudorandom states with classical keys and public-key encryption with copy-protected quantum decryption keys and classical public keys and ciphertexts, among other primitives, answering an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025).
papers.authors: Alper Cakan

papers.title: From FIPS to FPGA with LLM Agents: Measuring What Tests and Reviews Miss in Post-Quantum Cryptographic Hardware
papers.abstract: As LLM agents increasingly generate RTL alongside the tests and reviews that validate it, self-generated evidence is a weak foundation for trustworthy hardware. We present our seven-stage verification-gated workflow, evolved during a post-quantum design port, in which a gate counts only if shown able to fail on negative controls and fault mutants, and reviewer agents audit work before commit. We then audit this evidence with tool-selected netlist mutants, flaw replays, and formal checks. The flow ported an ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-65 accelerator to a 300 MHz Zynq UltraScale+ key-custody card: all six operations are byte-exact on the board, and it passes all 85 interface-applicable NIST ACVP cases (of 285) and 484 ML-DSA known answers. However, passing module tests overstate the verification strength. Across three RTL modules, existing simulation gates kill only 76% of 399 tool-selected netlist mutants; specification-derived tests guided by the survivors raise the fresh-draw decapsulation kill rate from 48% to 74%. In pre-registered single-model replays on flaws invisible to known-answer tests, undirected whole-design review catches two verifier flaws in only 3/6 and 1/6 sessions, whereas module-scoped review catches every known flaw in all 54 sessions. Even scoped review detects planted key-custody flaws in only 3/20 sessions, whereas formal checks (one added for the replay) flag every one. In this study, trustworthy agentic hardware needed author-independent mutants for test gates, module-level scoping for LLM review, and formal checks for custody invariants.
papers.authors: Jungmin Park, Eunha Kim, Wooseop Kim, Seongjoon Cho, Byungho Cha

papers.title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.
papers.authors: Meghana Aparna Sistla, Alaia Solko-Breslin, Somesh Jha, Aditya Kanade, Krishnamurthy Dj Dvijotham

papers.title: Signed, Valid, and Unauthorized: Authority Closure at the Trust Boundary Between Agent Commerce Protocols and Crypto Wallets
papers.abstract: Agent commerce protocols let software agents pay with stablecoins. A buyer approves a payee, asset, spending cap and time window, but the wallet signs an object whose effects depend on the contracts that consume it. Matching the displayed fields or simulating one payment can miss transfers that the signed object still permits. We define authority closure as the set of transfer sequences that holding the signed object can enable. A wallet object respects the mandate when every such sequence meets the buyer's constraints. We characterize when wallet objects can satisfy this property and implement Closure, a wallet-side checker covering 13 families of signed objects. In an evaluation of 2,130 generated objects and 62,979 execution programs, 265 objects with an observed violation passed both a field-and-expiry check and an address allow-list. Under the test model, Closure rejected all 1,680 objects with an observed violation and accepted the remaining 450. In two local checkouts using the x402 reference client, approved payments settled and Closure refused requests outside the mandate before signing. The median decision time was at most 12 microseconds per family.
papers.authors: Shengwei You, Aditya Joshi, Andrey Kuehlkamp, Jarek Nabrzyski

papers.title: Products of Distinguisher Hulls
papers.abstract: The distinguisher hull of two distributions is the convex hull of the pairs of acceptance probabilities of tests in a specified class. We study its behavior under independent products for size-bounded Boolean circuits. We derive a geometric consequence of Dwork and Tankala's supersimulator theorem (FOCS 2026), giving a substantially different proof of approximate product containment for distinguisher hulls. In particular, our construction uses nonadaptive sampling in place of adaptive score corrections.
papers.authors: John Paul Steinberger, Zhe Zhang

papers.title: Detecting Formation-Preserving GNSS Spoofing of UAV Swarms through Transmitter Parallax in Pseudorange and Doppler
papers.abstract: Swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) detect Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) spoofing by checking the drones' reported positions against their known formation. Formation-preserving spoofing evades this check: in GNSS-WASP, one transmitter per satellite, a few kilometres away, shifts the whole swarm while keeping its formation. We show that such an attack still leaves a trace below the position level. Because the transmitters are close, each drone sees them under a slightly different angle, and this parallax bends the signal arrival times across a 90 m swarm by 20-40 cm for a transmitter at 5 km, whatever delays the attacker applies. We propose a likelihood ratio test that reads this trace from the pseudoranges and Doppler every drone already measures, with all clocks and attacker delays unknown and no extra antennas. In simulations with real GPS and Galileo orbits and white receiver noise, 16 drones detect GNSS-WASP at 5 km in 13-60% of 10 s windows in straight flight and in every window during a formation turn with a precise Doppler receiver, where the countermeasure proposed with GNSS-WASP detects at most 5%. The same test also catches single-transmitter and ground-array spoofing.
papers.authors: Minseok Park, Joon Soo Yoo

papers.title: VisualJevBench: A Benchmark and Black-Box Attacks for Visual Typed Decision Models
papers.abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs) return structured decisions instead of generating free-text responses, enabling fast and cheap decisions in real-world applications. Recent support for image inputs extends Jev, a representative TDM, to visual decision-making. We refer to this setting as Visual Jev. However, red teaming of Visual Jev leaves two gaps: a systematic evaluation of direct image manipulations is lacking, and universal visual attacks remain underexplored. To address these gaps, we introduce VisualJevBench, a benchmark for evaluating the adversarial robustness of Visual Jev. It comprises 800 images and 3,200 questions across eight scenarios and four visual attack surfaces: typographic manipulation, visual evidence spoofing, target selection interference, and geometric transformation. We also introduce Adaptive Black-Box Parameter Search (ABPS), a lightweight framework that uses typed-output feedback to find effective image manipulations. ABPS supports both image-specific attacks and universal attacks that transfer to unseen images and tasks in new scenarios without further optimization. Extensive experiments on jev-1.14.0 show that image-specific attacks achieve an attack success rate (ASR) of up to 69.6%, while universal attacks achieve an average ASR of 33.15% on unseen images. Geometric transformations achieve an average ASR of 40.09% in cross-scenario transfer.
papers.authors: Li Zeng, Yeqi Zeng, Hengkai Liang, Shiguo Wang, Meng Xie, Zeyu Ye, Jinheng Zhang, Xianlong Wang, Ziqi Zhou, Hangtao Zhang

papers.title: Visual Attribution Limits and Graded Provenance Auditing in Commercial Video-Generation APIs
papers.abstract: Commercial video-generation APIs bill by model and tier, while intermediaries could substitute cheaper models, lower tiers, or cached clips. What can a delivered file establish about its origin? We combine measurements of passive attribution and cryptographic provenance into a graded audit. We test attribution probes and zero-shot detectors under re-encoding, downscaling, and frame-rate changes, and survey C2PA and GB 45438 metadata across 19 commercial endpoints. Only authenticated provenance supports accusations: tier contradictions or duplicate signed instances under fresh-generation contracts, excluding retries and idempotent returns. Unverifiable signed-endpoint deliveries trigger original-file demands under pass-through clauses; archive-reuse and delivery-parameter screens support review only. Six-model container and bitstream accuracy falls from 83.9% on raw files to 45.3% after uniform re-encoding, using different feature sets. Subsampling real references from 24 to 3 fps raises pooled D3 AUROC from 0.845 to 0.988. Only BytePlus authenticates tier claims under our pinned policy, including 187/187 audited deliveries across three Seedance tiers; tested remuxing and re-encoding leave processed Seedance files unverifiable. The audit identifies authenticated contradictions in 100/100 raw 720p signed tier-swap cases, with zero observed false flags on the tested honest pools.
papers.authors: Haocheng Mei, Yuchuan Tian, Yingte Shu, Chao Xu, Kai Han, Hanting Chen, Yunhe Wang

papers.title: When Suspicion Adds Up: A Stochastic Framework for Optimizing Honeypot-Based Insider-Threat Detection
papers.abstract: Insider threats pose security risks when employees or other trusted users misuse their access to organizational systems. Detecting these threats is difficult because harmful activity can resemble routine behavior. Honeypots, or decoy resources monitored for suspicious interactions, can provide evidence of potentially malicious activity. We develop a decision framework that models evidence accumulation through honeypot interactions using a continuous-time Markov chain and jointly selects honeypot counts and monitoring horizons to minimize expected losses from malicious activity and false detections. For thresholds of two and three interactions, we derive closed-form true- and false-detection probabilities and expected detection times conditional on detection within the monitoring horizon. We characterize boundary cases and establish stochastic-ordering results. Our numerical results highlight the value of the proposed framework across different settings.
papers.authors: Saharnaz Mehrani, Lujia Zhan, Mohsen Emadikhiav, Payman Dehghanian

papers.title: Causal Overtaking in Fair Transaction Ordering
papers.abstract: Fair transaction ordering protocols aim to mitigate front-running using replica-local arrival orders, but prior work often assumes a single submission origin for each responsive transaction. We identify causal overtaking, in which corrupted replicas observe a target and submit identical signed copies of a responsive transaction through multiple client entries. The copies' first arrivals at different replicas can collectively provide ordering support that no individual path achieves, allowing the response to execute before its target. We formalize a class of receipt-order protocols, including Themis, characterize the timing and network conditions under which the attack is feasible, and show that delayed gossip does not rule it out. We further prove that, under our network model, histories requiring opposite transaction orders can produce identical receipt evidence. Thus, receipt-only mechanisms cannot always preserve earlier-submission priority while preventing responsive overtaking. We propose a mitigation and analyze its assumptions and limitations. Finally, we evaluate the attack and mitigation on Themis through simulations driven by AWS and WonderProxy latency measurements.
papers.authors: Haozhe Feng, Di Wu, Jian Liu

papers.title: Signed but Unbound: The Authority Gap Between Agent Commerce Mandates and Crypto Wallet Signatures
papers.abstract: When an artificial intelligence agent pays with a stablecoin, the commerce protocol can specify the merchant, order, amount, and facilitator. The token contract enforces the fields the wallet signs. We call the difference the authority gap, define nine constraint classes, and derive them for 12 authorization configurations, including Coinbase's deployed Commerce Payments Protocol. All 31,800 trials on local copies of deployed contract code match the derivation. A controlled comparison shows that committing the terms in the signed nonce binds the order. When the facilitator submits a payment to a merchant account without code, binding the facilitator requires a separate recipient contract. Of 26,653 sampled USD Coin authorizations redeemed on Base, 98.7% followed a path that any holder of the signature could redeem. We prove sufficient conditions for a recipient contract to enforce the signed mandate under a trusted signer and show which recipient a wallet displays. MandateLock, a minimal implementation for immediate payments, rejects all 10,800 modified mandates on deployed token code and accepts signatures from two independent signers. It uses 25% more gas than a transfer that only the recipient can submit.
papers.authors: Shengwei You, Aditya Joshi, Andrey Kuehlkamp, Jarek Nabrzyski

papers.title: Ask in the Crowd: Differentially Private LLM Inference via Dummy-Augmented Shuffling
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as LLM-as-a-Service (LLMaaS), where user queries are sent to remote LLMs for inference, raising severe privacy concerns about the exposure of sensitive user inputs. Differentially private inference mitigates these risks by injecting noise into input embeddings. However, existing methods struggle to balance privacy and utility, as stronger privacy protection often leads to substantial accuracy degradation in LLM inference. In this work, we propose DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference framework that protects user queries by hiding the real query among client-generated dummy queries. All queries are randomly shuffled before being sent to the server, preventing direct identification of the user's true intent. To improve inference efficiency, we exploit the shared-prefix structure among queries and reuse transformer key--value (KV) caches during decoding. We analyze the privacy guarantee of DP-SPD and evaluate its utility on classification and generation tasks, as well as its privacy protection under QIA, EIA, and GPT-based attacks. Experimental results show that our method achieves strong inference-time privacy protection and near-plaintext utility while improving inference efficiency through shared-prefix KV-cache reuse.
papers.authors: Zhihao Liu, Zixiong Guo, Shuo Shao, Yu He, Wenli Wang, Meihui Chen, Di Wang, Yuke Hu

papers.title: Erasing the Wrong Thing: Conditional Attribute Leakage and Concept Erasure in Shared Foundation-Model Embeddings
papers.abstract: Medical-image embeddings are increasingly shared in place of raw images for authorized downstream tasks, yet they may reveal sensitive attributes. Standard concept-erasure methods target population-level guardedness. However, we prove that, when binary task and sensitive labels are associated, global and task-conditional linear guardedness cannot both hold while a nonzero linear task signal is preserved, so global erasure must either eliminate that signal or retain task-conditional linear leakage. We further show how global erasure affects linear readers' discrimination between positive and negative samples with different sensitive attributes, deriving an approximate closed-form prediction of its utility cost from pre-erasure statistics. Motivated by this conflict, we introduce Task-Conditional LEACE (TC-LEACE), a closed-form variant of LEACE that enforces linear guardedness within each task stratum of its fitting data. We evaluate four vision foundation models on 85 CelebA attribute pairs spanning a broad range of associations. After LEACE, conditional leakage persists across all four encoders, the discrepancy between marginal and conditional audits increases with association strength, and predicted utility costs track observed losses. We then examine hospital chest radiographs using three foundation models, including two biomedical models, in which chest-tube status is strongly associated with diagnosis. Although a marginal attack on LEACE-erased embeddings underperforms a diagnosis-only reference, chest-tube status remains detectable within diagnosis strata. TC-LEACE recovers most of LEACE's linear task-utility loss while keeping task-conditional leakage within a prespecified margin of LEACE's.
papers.authors: Haijun He, Fei Li, Donghong Ji, Junjun He

papers.title: Passing NPCR Without Diffusion: Exact Signatures, a Detection Benchmark and an Audit of Published Image Ciphers
papers.abstract: NPCR, the share of ciphertext bytes changed by a one-pixel plaintext change, is reported for nearly every image cipher as evidence of diffusion, with 99.61% the target. Several mechanisms produce values near it, and the mean does not say which. We separate three regimes: no propagation, one round of forward and backward chaining linear over addition or XOR, and independent ciphertexts. For the second an exact count applies. After a least-significant-bit change its mean asymptotically matches the independent-ciphertext reference, while its spread without cancellation is about five to twenty times larger. In simulation, the one-sided NPCR test of Wu, Noonan and Agaian flags one-round additive, mixed and S-box chaining in 2-4% of papers; read in both directions, the same five values flag at least 99.9%. Two-sided testing does the detecting; the spread and the other signatures help diagnose the structure. We then audit twenty-one published schemes. The count matches a reimplementation of one published diffusion layer on every trial and accounts for its reported table, the signatures show two schemes whose printed specifications cannot produce their reported values, and find that three of our own report plain-versus-cipher values and fall to two chosen images; ten more change their encryption material with the plaintext or per encryption, so their NPCR mostly reflects that change. A released checker applies the signatures to published tables, showing what a table measures within stated assumptions; it does not certify security.
papers.authors: Mua'ad Alfarajat

papers.title: Side-Channel Analysis of the RP2350 Challenge 2
papers.abstract: Bug bounty programs and community challenges have become an established mechanism to incentivize collective action to improve security. In essence, these can be considered as crowd-sourcing mechanisms where participants carry the risk twice over: performing the work in addition to having it officially accepted, which at times can be tied to unacceptable terms. Consequently, independent assessments and publications that are free from third party obligations remain important to highlight deficiencies in implementations of public significance. We consider the RP2350 side-channel analysis challenge and its hardened Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) implementation to be of reasonable importance to justify such an approach, especially so since the presented challenge remained unsolved for more than a year. In our paper, we present our analysis, demonstrating comprehensive leakage detection, plaintext dependence, and key extraction from the challenge implementation. Our work presents concerning weaknesses in the implementation that contradict the challenge authors' claims. We hope by openly sharing this analysis to motivate further public scrutiny.
papers.authors: Nikhil Tattikota, Vincent Immler

papers.title: TRACE-5G: Trust-Aware Runtime Attestation and Continuous Enforcement for 5G User Equipment
papers.abstract: The standard 5G Authentication and Key Agreement protocol (5G-AKA) authenticates subscriber credentials but does not verify the integrity of user equipment (UE). Existing literature includes admission-time device-certificate authentication and Trusted Platform Module (TPM)-based measured-boot attestation, which can additionally verify that the UE presents enrolled device credentials and boots into an approved state. However, these checks do not reveal whether harmful unauthorized software is executed after admission. We present TRACE-5G, which continuously verifies the UE's runtime software state and uses the resulting trust state to control network access. TRACE-5G retains the pre-admission certificate and boot checks, and in addition places the admitted UE in restricted connectivity while runtime integrity is verified. Linux Integrity Measurement Architecture (IMA) records runtime software measurements, TPM PCR (Platform Configuration Register) cryptographically accumulates them, and Keylime, a remote-attestation framework, repeatedly evaluates TPM and IMA evidence against enrolled references. A Trusted result grants full access on the existing PDU session, but an Untrusted result withholds or removes full access and causes network deregistration. We implement TRACE-5G on an srsRAN/Open5GS testbed with a hardware TPM2.0 UE and core-side firewall enforcement. Across ten trusted trials, Level 2 access was established in 9--12s. Across ten untrusted trials, promotion was consistently withheld; in a representative trace, restrictive policy was applied within 5ms of the Untrusted decision and UE-context release completed within 1.670s. TRACE-5G extends UE trust beyond admission without any modification of the standardized 5G protocols.
papers.authors: Al Nahian Bin Emran, Rajendra Paudyal, Rajendra Upadhyay, Arupjyoti Bhuyan, Duminda Wijesekera

papers.title: Release-Bound Withdrawal Authorization for Bitcoin Custody
papers.abstract: A compromised cryptocurrency withdrawal backend can request signatures on unauthorized payments. Previously signed transactions may remain spendable after pause or become spendable again after a reorganization. Release-Bound Withdrawal Authorization (RBWA) orders permits against pause in a replicated journal and restores exposure when its closing evidence disappears from Bitcoin's active chain. An optional route delays large payouts and permits independent cold recovery. Direct payments confirm in one block on regtest, and staged payments confirm in three or seven at delays of two or six. After rollback, a replayed recovery can win or lose to an already exported mature payout. Authenticated receipts can revoke one signing lease in a shared wallet. In matched synthetic schedules, probes reduce permits through compromised leases from 20 to 9 out of 33, with one false fence. Two held-out HTTP workloads find equal fixed-threshold precision for boosted audit and probe-augmented detectors. The audit fields already expose the probe authentication outcome. Live tests verify an exact maintenance exception and add a file marker as a distinct source. The marker fences a compromised lease that RPC-only audit misses. Audit with the same file-read evidence also fences a reader who bypasses the probe. The results tie the benefit of active probing to which evidence the operator can obtain.
papers.authors: Jian Cui, Rui Zhu, Haixu Tang

papers.title: Mutable State in Enrich-by-Need Security Protocol Analysis
papers.abstract: Security protocol analysis has emphasized message-passing, as this is how different principals interact in authentication, key exchange, and similar functionalities. However, in many protocols a principal also maintains mutable state that limits what actions its local sessions may take; this cross-session state is altered by other local sessions. In this paper we show how to represent this cross-session mutable state in the strand space approach to symbolic protocol analysis, and how to implement the resulting ideas in the Cryptographic Protocol Shapes Analyzer CPSA. The key theory is expressed in two axioms characterizing state, plus protocol-specific rules. It leads to tight, specific characterizations of protocol behavior in relevant cases, and aids in developing correct protocols relying on cross-session mutable state.
papers.authors: Joshua D Guttman, Paul D Rowe, Eben Blaisdell

papers.title: Living off the Local Model: Abusing Browser-Embedded Language Models for Post-Exploitation
papers.abstract: Browsers now ship local language models to ordinary endpoints. Google includes Gemini Nano in Chrome to enable productivity features such as summarization, with inference running entirely on the device. These browser-embedded models provide new living-off-the-land opportunities for attackers, each instance a potential post-exploitation engine already installed, signed by the vendor, and invisible to network monitoring. The Gemini model is multimodal, capable of processing files, analyzing screenshots, or conversing with an attacker. We show that it can be driven from the host using only interpreters that ship with the operating system and find that the one-time user-activation check before the model is downloaded is easily satisfied with a simulated click or bypassed entirely.We measure and report the current model's ability to identify credentials on the host, detect PII in email, classify images, and call custom tools. We combine these capabilities and use the model to carry out a simulated cyber operation: reading a password from a webcam image, unlocking an encrypted archive, triaging the contents, and staging a private key for exfiltration, end-to-end without user-interaction.
papers.authors: William Fleshman, Joseph Lucas

papers.title: PriTabICL: Differentially Private Tabular In-Context Learning with Task-Aligned Cluster-Wise Synthesis
papers.abstract: Tabular in-context learning (TabICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to predict target records using a handful of labeled demonstrations in their prompts. However, these demonstrations often contain sensitive personal information. Differential privacy (DP) offers principled protection, but noise-based methods introduce substantial noise, distorting the feature-label relationships essential for accurate prediction, especially as data dimensionality grows. In this work, we study DP data synthesis for generating privacy-preserving TabICL demonstrations. We identify two limitations of directly applying general-purpose DP synthesis to entire datasets: modeling a global distribution can obscure local structure and minority patterns in heterogeneous data, while measuring broad attribute dependencies under a limited privacy budget can reduce the accuracy available for relationships most relevant to prediction. More broadly, global statistical fidelity may fail to preserve heterogeneous structures needed by downstream predictive and generative models. To address these challenges, we propose PriTabICL, a general framework compatible with existing DP synthesis algorithms. It partitions records into DP clusters and synthesizes each independently, using a fixed feature-target workload to prioritize prediction-relevant statistical relationships. At inference, each query is routed to a DP cluster, and demonstrations are sampled from its synthetic dataset without additional privacy loss for the original records. Experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods across heterogeneous datasets. In particular, one of our instantiations, PriTabICL-PrivSyn, improves over global PrivSyn in 8 out of 12 settings and outperforms existing private TabICL approaches in nearly all evaluated settings. Open-source code is available.
papers.authors: Syed Ahzaz Shah, Evan Bramblett, Héber H. Arcolezi, Chen Gong, Qianqian Tong, Xiaochen Li

papers.title: Attacks and Defenses in Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems with Hop-by-Hop Task Decomposition and Delegation
papers.abstract: Decentralized multi-agent LLM systems enable independently administered agents, each with its own operator, model, memory, and configuration, to collaborate on complex tasks without centralized coordination. Agents autonomously decompose tasks, execute subtasks and delegate remaining work to peers, enabling scalability and eliminating single points of failure. However, decentralization also introduces significant security challenges, as no single entity has complete visibility into task execution or the authority to enforce correct behavior across agents. In this paper, we systematize threats from malicious agents in decentralized multi-agent systems and propose mitigation techniques. We first design and evaluate attacks against integrity, availability, and confidentiality, demonstrating that a single malicious agent can cause up to 100% task failure, inflate token consumption and runtime by up to 7.7x and 3.2x, respectively, and exfiltrate up to 94% of relevant prior tasks from benign agents. We then present a cryptographic protocol that produces an irrefutable verified execution trace of every action taken in the system and develop an auditor that analyzes these traces to detect and attribute malicious behavior. Evaluations on HiddenBench using gpt-6.1-sol and Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 show that our protocol incurs negligible latency overhead, while the auditor detects and correctly attributes 98% of attacks, including those that comply with the protocol.
papers.authors: Matthew D. Laws, Maria Lazou, Alina Oprea, Cristina Nita-Rotaru

papers.title: Text-Aware, Vision-Blind: How Multimodal Image Editing Systems Handle Unsafe Inputs
papers.abstract: Multimodal image generation systems have made rapid progress and increasingly emphasize content safety. However, their safety mechanisms tend to rely on a single modality and lack joint consideration of both visual content and text prompts, particularly in instruction-guided image editing, where the uploaded image may itself carry risk. We thus introduce EditSafetyBench, a benchmark that measures system-level safety awareness of advanced image editing systems, containing 5,940 image-instruction pairs, covering safe and unsafe images across 11 risk categories and three edit intents. We then probe the benchmark dataset on four systems, including Gemini, GPT, Qwen API, and Qwen Local. Based on our evaluation, we observe a systematic text-vision safety mismatch: Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1\% and 81.6\% cases containing unsafe-intent editing prompts, while only refusing 24.2\% and 22.4\% cases with both unsafe images and neutral instructions. At the category level, most risks are considered inconsistently by different systems, e.g., GPT allows 70.4\% editing attempts of unsafe political content while Gemini only allows 34.8\%. Notably, sexual content shows the strongest visual sensitivity, likely benefiting from mature NSFW identification works. Our findings highlight the need for safety guardrails that jointly reason over both visual and textual modalities in image editing systems.
papers.authors: Ziqing Yang, Yixin Wu, Michael Backes, Yang Zhang

papers.title: GEOHunter: Mapping a Generative Engine Optimization Network in the Wild
papers.abstract: Generative engines synthesize retrieved web pages into answers, recommendations, and rankings. Generative engine optimization (GEO) services sell visibility in these answers by publishing promotional articles on user-generated-content (UGC) platforms for paying clients. Such promotion raises concerns in medical and financial domains, where misleading advice can cause harm. To study the severity of this problem, we measure one such paid-content operation across three major Chinese UGC platforms, uncovering 1,985 accounts associated with the network comprising 466,357 inferred promotional placements. We find that the network promotes products across diverse categories through a growing pool of accounts, conducting coordinated campaigns spanning months across multiple platforms while evolving its listicle content over time. Across nine generative engines from both the US and China, we find that 4.5% to 20% of retrievable cited pages are attributable to the network, depending on how strictly attribution is drawn. On eight of these engines, its clients are named in 52% of answers, against 68% for category leaders. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of UGC GEO placement at influencing generative engine outcomes, and reveals content-level defenses as insufficient against coordinated UGC placements, where account-level and platform-level signals are necessary for proper defense.
papers.authors: Sean Tang, Peiran Wang, Ying Li, Esha Shivakumar, Tao Meng, Yuan Tian

papers.title: Backtracking Agent Applications Security Incidents
papers.abstract: Agent applications are increasingly deployed, yet agent-specific attacks pose real threats to them. Upon a security incident, organizations backtrack to identify the CEP (compromise entry point), remediate the damage, and prevent its recurrence. The main artifacts available for backtracking are trajectory logs, which record agent functionalities, and source code; app(lication)-specific function call logs are often fairly limited. However, trajectory logs are at the agent functionality abstraction layer, while the CEP candidates are function calls at the app code execution layer. Due to this semantic gap, the analyst needs to manually inspect the relevant code for each CEP candidate to infer its corresponding agent functionality. In this work, we present Origin, a backtracking tool for the analyst to submit a small number of queries to identify CEPs that existing tools cannot provide. Our approach poses two challenges: (1) define the intermediate abstraction that captures the mapping relationships between the two semantic layers; (2) determine the region-to-variable mapping for constructing the cross-layer graph defined in the intermediate abstraction. Each region is a specific group of agent functionalities. Origin addresses the challenges by (1) the cross-layer dependency graph (CLDG) that connects region-inferred functions at the semantic level to the variables in the low-level taint propagation subgraph, plus the associated query language, and (2) the region inference algorithm. Case studies on five popular agent applications across eight attack incidents show that an analyst using Origin correctly identifies all the CEPs.
papers.authors: Yicheng Cai, Taegyu Kim, Peng Liu

papers.title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions
papers.abstract: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.
papers.authors: Xuankun Rong, Xinhao Deng, Wenzhang Jiang, Ziheng Peng, Siyuan Liang, Wenke Huang, Pablo Arbelaez, Mang Ye

papers.title: ChronoPatch: Black-Box Energy-Latency Attacks on Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as generative inference services, where autoregressive decoding makes response length a key determinant of latency and computational cost. This creates an availability risk: adversarial visual inputs can prolong generation and increase serving overhead. Existing energy-latency attacks typically rely on gradients, logits, or token-level feedback, leaving open whether such risks persist when an attacker observes only the final response. We present ChronoPatch, a black-box attack that induces prolonged VLM generation requiring only the final response. It discovers visual delay anchors through response-length-guided evolutionary search, then minimizes perturbation magnitude through subspace-calibrated decision-based optimization. Across four open-source VLMs, ChronoPatch increases inference latency by 47.86%--293.34% and GPU energy consumption by 41.44%--249.70% under a 5% spatial budget. It also induces more repetitive outputs, as reflected by increased n-gram repetition ratios. On three commercial VLM APIs, ChronoPatch increases response length by 37.6%--81.5% and client-observed latency by 1.82x--2.29x under query budgets of 500 per API. These results reveal a generation-based availability risk that persists under final-response-only access and motivate generation-aware safeguards for deployed generative AI services.
papers.authors: Jiawei Xing, Li Wang, Xiangtao Meng, Chuanchao Zang, Rui Wen, Zheng Li

papers.title: Question, Then Affirm: Restoring Commitment Does Not Restore Refusal
papers.abstract: We find that safeguards for image generation can be bypassed without changing what a message says. A sign stating a harmful proposition is blocked, but the same proposition phrased as a question and followed by a check mark is generated, even though the resulting image endorses the original claim. On a 300-case challenge set, gpt-image-2 returns images for 43.3% of question-affirmation requests versus 16.3% of direct statements, with 41.3% versus 15.3% of cases yielding images that endorse the original proposition. We define this as Deferred Semantic Commitment (DSC): commitment is withdrawn by the question and restored by a separate element, while safety behavior follows only the withdrawal. To investigate why, we study an open-weight language model and find that re-endorsement only partially reverses the refusal-related change introduced by questioning. These findings reveal a mismatch between recovered meaning and refusal behavior, motivating safeguards that assess the completed message rather than its individual elements.
papers.authors: Haoyang Xu, Qirui Wang, Liuwan Zhu

papers.title: Hardening JavaScript Programs against LLM-Based Vulnerability Detection
papers.abstract: JavaScript programs are often distributed as source code, so attackers can analyze them for vulnerabilities. LLM-based vulnerability detection agents now make this analysis much easier. To mitigate this emerging threat, we present AntiAgent, a defense that lets developers harden their programs against such detection agents. AntiAgent transforms a program before release to impede an agent's analysis. To find effective transformations, AntiAgent evolves a corpus of programs with known vulnerabilities and traces how a detection agent analyzes each evolved version. It keeps the versions on which the agent misses or misreports the vulnerability and extracts their transformations into reusable rules. To protect a new program, AntiAgent carefully divides the task between an LLM and the rules, so that the transformations adapt to the program while preserving its semantics. We evaluate AntiAgent on real-world JavaScript applications against four detection agents, including Claude Code and Codex. AntiAgent reduces the number of vulnerabilities that each agent detects by 52.0-60.7%, outperforming the conventional obfuscator JS-Obfuscator and the LLM-based transformation method FPA on every agent. The transformed programs pass all project tests, indicating that AntiAgent preserves the original program semantics. The transformation rules also remain effective on vulnerability types absent from the corpus and on programs written in another language like Python.
papers.authors: Zhenhao Tian, Jintong Yu, Jingwei Feng, Jianwei Zhuge, Penghui Li

papers.title: Measuring Hallucination in Large Language Models for Cyber Threat Intelligence: An Exploratory Study
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in cyber threat intelligence (CTI) tasks, such as summarization and question answering. However, they may produce hallucinations, false or misleading content not grounded in the source text, which can mislead analysts and corrupt downstream security decisions. This paper presents an exploratory measurement study of hallucinations in LLM-based CTI. We introduce HalluVision, a reproducible framework that generates LLM outputs, extracts domain-specific entities using a fine-tuned named entity recognition model, and evaluates factual consistency using multiple similarity metrics. Using 4,940 real-world cybersecurity articles, we measure hallucinations in outputs from two commercial LLMs and one open-weight LLM. Measurements are validated against 100 human-annotated outputs and two established faithfulness detectors. Results show that semantic similarity aligns with human judgments, whereas entity-based metrics exhibit limited agreement. Differences between models are concentrated in question answering, while entity extraction quality limits what entity-level metrics can reveal.
papers.authors: Seungho Song, Donggyu Lee, Jaehan Kim, Jiyoung Choi, Jinwoo Kim

papers.title: AZOWL AgentOps: Task-Scoped Governance for Deployed Agent Applications
papers.abstract: AZOWL AgentOps provides shared governance for deploying agents and delegating work to them. Human and agent senders can exchange messages or explicitly delegate a business task. Accepted work has a stable identifier that links the sender's authority, the assigned runner, any required approval, and result evidence. The default enrolled customer PC profile is read-only. We compare AZOWL components with a configured LangGraph application in 28 synthetic runs across four paired pilots. Original AZOWL services checked work admission, recipient routing, and workflow prerequisites in isolated tests. The configured LangGraph application supplied business task and dispatch records in application code. Both configurations recorded zero business tasks in dialogue, rejected unauthorized agent handoffs, and issued zero writes when an approved delivery address changed. AZOWL's scope gate, exercised as a component, requested approval again on the same task. A product probe reused one registered provider across two workflows and checked prerequisite enforcement for ticket-task submission. The paired protected writes, including ticket creation, used mock providers. Of two deployed PC inventory reads with verified receipts, we traced the 0.6.57 run from submission through runner pickup and tool execution to the receipt, with matching local and central artifact hashes. A separate deployed GRC audit followed an operator-driven ticket lifecycle on sample records.
papers.authors: Taeoh Hong

papers.title: UniReFP: Robust Unified Fingerprinting for Vision Models against Cross-Task Repurposing Attacks
papers.abstract: We identify, for the first time, a new model modification attack--the cross-task model repurposing attack--that can render fingerprints generated by existing model fingerprinting approaches inapplicable. To address this challenge, we propose UniReFP--a novel unified model fingerprinting framework applicable to diverse vision models across different tasks--that utilizes ownership evidence in a shared class-level semantic space rather than original task-specific output space, enabling effective ownership verification when a protected model is repurposed across tasks with heterogeneous output formats. Specifically, UniReFP constructs a surrogate classifier by repurposing the protected model, enabling fingerprints to be generated independently of the original task-dependent output space of the protected model. Moreover, it optimizes grouped fingerprints to encode ownership evidence: fingerprints within the same group are encouraged to induce consistent semantic responses and intermediate representations on the surrogate classifier, while producing dispersed responses on independently trained reference classifiers. During verification, UniReFP uses a task-aware semantic projection mechanism to map heterogeneous suspect-model outputs into unified semantic-presence vectors, and determines ownership by measuring inner-group consistency. Extensive experimental results validate the effectiveness of UniReFP, consistently showing superior performance under cross-task repurposing attacks, commonly studied model modification attacks, and even their combinations.
papers.authors: Ziye Geng, Guang Yang, Yihang Chen, Lingfeng Yao, Xing Shi, Miao Pan, Xin Fu, Changqing Luo

papers.title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
papers.abstract: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.
papers.authors: LingSante MedGuard Team

papers.title: ToolPulse: Side-Channel Eavesdropping on Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that translate user requests into sequences of local tool invocations. While prior cache-based side-channel attacks target the locally deployed models, they typically require the adversary to share model-related components or hardware resources with the victim's inference process. These assumptions do not apply to the predominant agentic settings, in which commercial LLMs execute on vendor-controlled infrastructure. We show that agentic execution exposes a more practical attack surface: although inference remains remote, tools are executed on the user's machine and commonly rely on shared system libraries. In this paper, we first systematically evaluate Flush+Reload and Prime+Probe for monitoring agentic tool invocations. Our evaluation across three hardware platforms shows that Flush+Reload enables accurate, real-time tool monitoring, whereas Prime+Probe, despite supporting cross-VM attacks, incurs prohibitive monitoring overhead and suffers from cache-set aliasing. We present ToolPulse, a cache-based side-channel eavesdropping framework against tool-using agents. We first design the Tool Recovery Attack to reconstruct an agent's tool-execution workflow. We evaluate the Tool Recovery Attack on 11 LLMs across Codex and Claude Code. It consistently reconstructs tool workflows, with the lowest F1 score exceeding 93%. We further demonstrate two attack scenarios enabled by the recovered traces. Task Profiling Attack infers user intent across two Terminal-Bench task categories and the Trigger Localization Attack identifies sensitive tool calls in encryption/decryption and model training/inference workloads. Even under substantial system noise on a server shared by approximately 20 users, both Task Profiling Attack and Trigger Localization Attack maintain high accuracy.
papers.authors: Zihao Dan, Jinyu Zhang, Jinzhao Lian, Yun Chen, Shinan Liu

papers.title: Verified Netlist-to-RTL Recovery with LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Gate-level netlists circulate among IP integrators and foundries and can be extracted from chips. Reverse engineering them into readable register-transfer-level (RTL) code would help an adversary understand and modify a design, but remains difficult because word-level operations are scattered across many gates. Large language models (LLMs) can write and optimize RTL, but often fail to recover it from a whole netlist. We propose LOCA (LOgic Cone Attack), an LLM-based attack that divides an anonymized netlist into logic cones, has parallel agents rewrite them, and assembles compact RTL. Each cone contains the complete next-state logic of a group of related registers, giving an agent a small, meaningful task. Of five partitioning methods tested, only grouped cones lead to recovery. LOCA keeps only RTL proven equivalent to the netlist and measures its quality by compression. Function-preserving obfuscation does not stop LOCA on the tested designs, whereas unknown keys or hidden cell functions prevent it from proving recovery of the original design. Across 21 model-design pairs, LOCA recovers 17, versus 6 with whole-netlist prompting. Per-run recovery across models rises from 5% to 74%, at a median cost below one dollar with a low-cost model.
papers.authors: Ahmet Efe, Recep Bugra Uludag, Ulya R. Karpuzcu

papers.title: SCARVA: Interpretable Agentic Reasoning in Software Supply-Chain Analysis
papers.abstract: Complex applications may inherit security vulnerabilities from their dependencies, though a vulnerable dependency does not necessarily endanger the application. Existing tools flag dependencies associated with public vulnerabilities, and more advanced ones analyze the call graph to assess whether the vulnerable code is reachable. However, these approaches are limited to specific programming languages and ecosystems. LLM agents are promising candidates for this task, yet they hallucinate, take shortcuts, and reward hack. As these behaviors are opaque, the agents' conclusions may not be trusted. We present SCARVA a framework designed to produce interpretable reports. SCARVA combines advanced agent reasoning with an evidence-collection methodology that assesses the agent's analysis and improves its trustworthiness. Specifically, the ANALYST performs a software security assessment while SCARVA records every tool call, file access, and web request. Then, one or more independent JUDGE agents inspect the ANALYST's result and produce an evidence-backed report. We evaluate SCARVA on 54 manually curated cases, balanced across exploitable, non-exploitable, and vulnerability-free projects, using both open-weight and frontier models. The best ANALYST model, Qwen 3.8, reaches 82% balanced accuracy and surpasses the evaluated proprietary models. Human annotation validates the JUDGE findings: Claude Opus 5.5 performs best, agreeing with annotators in 94% of claim checks. Finally, we discuss the most common failure modes of agents on supply-chain vulnerability assessment.
papers.authors: Tim Barsch, Bruno Nogueira, Tobias Wienand, Jan Fopma, Flavio Toffalini

papers.title: On the Reliability of CyberGym Evaluation: Task Material Consistency and Reference-Target Identity
papers.abstract: CyberGym evaluates vulnerability reproduction by checking whether a proof-of-concept input (PoC) crashes a vulnerable program version but not a fixed version. Interpreting this differential pass as successful reproduction requires consistent task materials and evidence that the PoC triggers the intended defect. We examine these requirements through a material audit of all 1,507 CyberGym tasks and an identity assessment of the final PoCs from one complete Level-1 GLM-5.3 run. Taking the defect associated with each reference crash report as the target, the audit assigns inconsistency labels to 338 tasks (22.4%) after correcting two labels identified by stratified blind review. The largest categories are coverage inconsistency (205 tasks) and descriptions and patches that jointly point to another defect (110 tasks). We assess PoC identity using an execution check, crash-signature matching, and LLM-assisted root-cause review. Of the 1,286 differential passes, the procedure assigns 89 non-target and 10 insufficient-evidence verdicts; requiring a target hit lowers the pass rate from 85.3% to 78.8%. Non-target verdicts also occur in tasks with no material inconsistency found: 39 of 1,052 differential passes (3.7%). Although the identity verdicts require independent validation, these findings motivate separate checks of task-material consistency and submission identity when interpreting vulnerability-reproduction scores.
papers.authors: Yule Ding, Hongzhen Wu

papers.title: ChainAgent: Automated Chainable Vulnerability Discovery in PHP Web Applications
papers.abstract: High-impact attacks on PHP web applications often chain limited-capability vulnerabilities with other flaws or intended behaviors. Discovering these chains requires identifying flaws and the dependencies enabling capability composition. Existing vulnerability discovery techniques analyze flaws in isolation, while attack planning assumes known components. This separation makes it difficult to discover previously unknown components whose security relevance becomes apparent only through their potential roles in an exploit chain. We present ChainAgent, a goal-directed LLM-agent framework that jointly discovers exploit-chain components and their capability dependencies in source code. Guided by an empirical study of 386 real-world web exploit chains, ChainAgent represents vulnerabilities and functional gadgets--intended program behaviors that can be repurposed in attacks--through preconditions and capabilities over security-relevant objects. Instead of discovering vulnerabilities first and constructing attack paths afterward, ChainAgent uses an evolving exploit graph to guide source-code inspection. It searches backward from unmet preconditions for capability producers and forward from discovered capabilities for functional gadgets that consume or amplify them. Object-centered chaining knowledge from our empirical study directs searches toward promising vulnerability classes, functional operations, and object accesses. We evaluate ChainAgent against Codex, a general-purpose coding agent, on 15 PHP applications across three shared LLM backends. ChainAgent achieves 42.02%--44.63% recall for goal-reaching components and recovers up to 4.4 times as many correct goal-reaching dependency edges as Codex. An additional evaluation of 30 real-world PHP applications identifies 20 vulnerabilities and 13 exploit chains, nine of which achieve remote code execution (RCE).
papers.authors: Xinyi Wang, Yeting Li, Shizhe Cui, Jiaming Guo, Qin Mai, Yecheng Sun, Hengyu Yang, Yujie Sun, Huina Chao, Yang Xiao, Feng Li, Wei Huo

papers.title: SplitReAlign: Partition-Aware Representation Realignment for Split Federated Unlearning
papers.abstract: Split federated learning (SFL) distributes neural networks across clients and a server, coupling class-specific knowledge across their representations. This coupling complicates split federated unlearning (SFU), where class-wise forgetting must remove target knowledge while preserving retained utility under heterogeneous representation spaces and asymmetric update constraints. We propose SplitReAlign, a partition-aware representation realignment framework for class-wise SFU. It constructs endpoint-specific discriminative subspaces coordinated through a shared semantic anchor, selectively realigning forgotten representations while penalizing changes outside the active subspaces. To accommodate asymmetric update constraints, SplitReAlign leverages gradients through frozen servers for Client-only updates and fixed client-feature statistics for Server-only guidance, while Joint updates optimize both partitions. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 under heterogeneous client distributions demonstrate that SplitReAlign achieves the lowest average gap to retraining among all compared methods across six settings. Notably, Server-only achieves the closest agreement with retraining on both datasets, highlighting the effectiveness of partition-aware guidance under restricted updates.
papers.authors: Jia Chen, Yecheng Lv, Xinrong Hu, Jun Bai

papers.title: Ties at the Top: A Point-in-Time Comparison of CVSS and EPSS at a Fixed Budget
papers.abstract: Organizations must decide which vulnerabilities warrant further analysis and protective action when the volume of published vulnerabilities exceeds their analytical capacity. We present a methodology for comparing vulnerability-prioritization strategies under an explicit resource constraint, represented by a fixed number of CVEs selected from a common eligible population. We apply this methodology to the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) and the Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS). For CVEs published in the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) from 17 March to 31 December 2025 and from 1 January to 31 March 2026 (Q1), we reconstruct each CVE's scores and status 30 days after NVD publication, using archived source data. Each cohort has one ranking per strategy at a 5% budget. Positives are CVEs added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog within 180 days after their decision day. The catalog is maintained by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). EPSS captures 16 of 40 positives in 2025, versus 5 for CVSS; alternative selections among tied CVEs cannot raise CVSS capture above 9. In Q1, CVSS captures 4 of 11 and EPSS 3, but tie-breaking can reverse this ordering. The score alone leaves most of each CVSS list undecided: the tie-breaking rule allocates 1,678 of 1,919 CVSS places in 2025 and 589 of 758 in Q1 among CVEs tied at score 9.8. Most chosen CVSS scores come from non-NVD providers; disabling those scores reduces CVSS capture from 5 to 1 in 2025 and from 4 to 0 in Q1. A fixed-budget comparison should therefore report its decision cutoff, eligible population, score provenance, and tie-breaking rule.
papers.authors: Gianluca Martinuz, Paolo Ceravolo

papers.title: SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities in real-world software without human intervention before the restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records, advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived a decade or more in widely used code were reported several times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages of a vulnerability's life, from report to fix and from disclosure to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the best-supported ones.
papers.authors: Amine Lbath, Manan Suri, Aurelien Delaitre, Vadim Okun, Massih-Reza Amini, Dinesh Manocha

papers.title: BlockJack: Cross-Tenant Redirection Fault Attacks on Paged KV Cache Address Translation in LLM Serving
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving frameworks accelerate inference by retaining previously computed states in a key-value (KV) cache. Paged serving frameworks such as vLLM organize this cache through block tables analogous to OS page tables, which map each request's logical KV blocks to physical KV blocks, forming a software-managed address translation layer. Although fault attacks such as Rowhammer have exploited OS page tables to redirect memory accesses, prior fault attacks on LLMs have largely targeted the data plane, i.e., model weights or KV-cache contents, leaving KV-cache mapping unexplored. We present BlockJack (i.e., Block Hijack), the first KV cache address-translation fault attack in LLM inference. By corrupting block-table entries, BlockJack redirects a request's KV cache reads to blocks assigned to another tenant's request without modifying model parameters, prompts, or cached KV states. It achieves both confidentiality violation (victim information appears in attacker responses) and integrity violation (attacker-supplied context steers victim answers). We study paged KV cache mappings in vLLM and formally characterize when redirect targets are predictable. Across seven models spanning the Qwen, Llama, Gemma, and Phi families, a faulted mapping exposes victim context. For the integrity attack, we examine how topic proximity, intra-topic divergence, and model behavior shape redirected responses. On a 248-scene medical benchmark, the integrity attack causes up to 41.1% of responses to recommend less urgent care, while still appearing consistent with the victim's question. We demonstrate physical feasibility of BlockJack with Rowhammer and subsequently evaluate assignment validation as a defense. Following responsible disclosure, vLLM and Sonar confirmed the vulnerability and proposed patches that we reviewed and validated.
papers.authors: Qifan Wang, Jeremy Boy, Jonas Sander, Yansong Gao, Hongsheng Hu, Ye Dong, Thomas Eisenbarth, David Oswald

papers.title: ALIoTh: Orchestrating Multi-Agent LLMs for Autonomous IoT Penetration Testing
papers.abstract: Penetration testing in Internet of Things (IoT) environments, especially those composed of various different devices, e.g., smart plugs, smart cameras, and smart doors, presents great challenges across the phases of information gathering, attack surface enumeration, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This paper introduces ALIoTh, a multi-agent, workflow-driven penetration testing framework that integrates Large Language Models agents within a Self-Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Self-RAG) architecture to autonomously identify and exploit vulnerabilities in IoT and Industrial-IoT (IIoT) environments. By leveraging state-of-the-art language models and orchestrating specialized agents via the LangGraph framework, ALIoTh dynamically plans and executes a full-spectrum offensive pipeline. This includes network, devices, and service enumeration, vulnerability assessment, payload generation, reverse shell deployment, and privilege escalation on each device. The Self-RAG mechanism equips expert agents with contextual access to IoT security knowledge, e.g., related documentation, tool manuals, and known attack techniques, enhancing their reasoning capabilities in scenarios involving multiple device exploitation and group policy manipulation.
papers.authors: Pironti Francesco Aurelio, Arena Luigi, Blefari Francesco, Lupinacci Matteo, Romeo Francesco, Maresca Alessio

papers.title: MetaScanner: An Empirical Study and Proactive Defense against Deceptive UI Attacks in Social VR
papers.abstract: Social virtual reality (VR) platforms have surged in popularity but continue to face significant security challenges, including privacy invasion and user manipulation. Yet, the security risks posed by deceptive content remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce four novel deceptive UI attacks that covertly manipulate social VR users into performing unintended actions without their awareness. We show how adversarial content creators can embed seemingly benign scripts and interactive elements within carefully designed virtual worlds, deceiving users into unknowingly carrying out harmful behaviors. We implemented these attacks on VRChat, a leading social VR platform, and an IRB-approved user study involving 30 participants confirmed their effectiveness. To mitigate these threats, we propose MetaScanner, a proactive analysis system that efficiently scans virtual world assets, including scripts and interactive objects, to identify suspicious or deceptive elements before users are exposed to them. We demonstrate that MetaScanner can successfully detect all threats in test worlds where the four attack scenarios were implemented. Additionally, MetaScanner shows its lightweight nature, with an average scanning time of 5 seconds across 38 real-world assets.
papers.authors: Junhee Lee, Seungwon Woo, Minseok Kim, Jongseop Kim, Kiyoung Kim, Hwanjo Heo, Jinwoo Kim

papers.title: User Perceptions of Deceptive In-Vehicle Infotainment User Interfaces
papers.abstract: Modern vehicles collect extensive data about drivers, passengers, and vehicle use, with privacy and consent decisions increasingly mediated through infotainment software. Although dark patterns have been widely studied in web, mobile, and e-commerce interfaces, little is known about how they appear in automotive infotainment systems or how users perceive them. We study this problem through Android Automotive OS (AAOS), conducting a three-phase empirical analysis. First, 26 HCI and privacy annotators audit four OEM AAOS emulators (Honda, Volvo, GM, and Polestar), documenting 17 dark-pattern types across 65 observations. Second, a user study with 100 participants compares OEM-specific implementations of five dark patterns across GMC, Honda, and Volvo, finding that implementation choices affect user perceptions. Third, an independent study with 49 participants compares automotive and e-commerce dark-pattern clips before and after a brief tutorial, showing that automotive's initial rating advantage largely collapses after instruction. Together, the studies identify a sophistication paradox: subtler dark patterns are less likely to trigger user suspicion and may therefore be harder to identify. These findings indicate that oversight should evaluate not just the presence but also the specific implementation of dark patterns.
papers.authors: Pedram MohajerAnsari, Iwinosa Aideyan, Anna Galeano, Arjun Arunasalam, Bart Knijnenburg, Richard Brooks, Mert D. Pesé

papers.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
papers.abstract: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.
papers.authors: Mengxiao Wang, Mahbub Alam, Kalyan Nakka, Nitesh Saxena

papers.title: Phantom of the Masquerade: Graph Neural Network-Based Detection of Masquerade Attacks in Controller Area Networks
papers.abstract: The lack of built-in security in controller area networks (CANs) exposes modern vehicles and industrial systems to masquerade attacks that can compromise safety and reliability. These attacks inject malicious messages that mimic legitimate communication patterns, making them difficult to detect using existing intrusion detection systems (IDS). Prior graph-based IDS approaches often rely on shallow embeddings that decouple representation learning from classification, which may limit their ability to fully exploit structural and signal-level information. In this paper, we propose PhantoMasq, a graph neural network (GNN)-based framework for detecting masquerade attacks in CAN systems.
