We prove that protocols with signature tokens can bypass this lower bound by designing a protocol that remains secure against up to a $\frac{2^{k+1}-1}{2^{k+2}-1}$-fraction of faults. In particular, with $k=\Theta(\log n)$, where $n$ denotes the number of parties, our protocol solves Byzantine Agreement in partial synchrony assuming only an honest majority. Conversely, we prove that $\Omega(\log n)$ signature tokens are necessary for such a result. Finally, for $k=1$, we prove that the fault-tolerance threshold of $3/7$ achieved by our protocol is the best possible.
papers.authors: Yuval Efron, Mahimna Kelkar, Saachi Mutreja, Tim Roughgarden

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Systemic Portfolio Analysis and Repair
papers.abstract: Financial institutions can be exposed to systemic risk through overlapping portfolios and common liquidity shocks, yet identifying and reducing these dependencies requires precisely the portfolio information that institutions are unwilling to reveal. We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first privacy-preserving framework combining system -level portfolio analysis with coordinated portfolio repair. Our approach uses secure multi-party computation (MPC), allowing mutually distrustful institutions to jointly identify systemic vulnerabilities and determine concrete portfolio adjustments without disclosing their underlying holdings. We provide both an MPC realization and a federated variant that moves fund-local computation outside MPC while retaining secure global coordination, and we analyze the additional leakage introduced by this federated design. We implement and evaluate the complete framework on real, publicly available portfolios. Across representative network profiles, private analysis completes in roughly 1–4 minutes and portfolio repair takes 2.6–8.8 hours in MPC and 13–21 minutes in the federated setting. Our results show that both private systemic-risk analysis and coordinated intervention are practically feasible with current MPC technology.
papers.authors: Martin Zbudila, Roozbeh Sarenche, Aysajan Abidin, Bart Preneel

papers.title: Adaptable Watermarking: Transforming Image Watermarking Models via Lightweight Adapters
papers.abstract: We explore the adaptability of neural image watermarking models; the extent to which one watermarking method can be transformed into another through lightweight adaptation. We introduce a framework that enables encoder-decoder watermarking architectures to become modular and upgradable, supporting multiple watermarking styles without re-training full models. Adaptation is performed by attaching a compact parameter-efficient adapter and fine-tuning under a multi-domain residual alignment loss (spatial, gradient, and frequency) while preserving bit accuracy via a secret-loss term. We evaluate this approach across a suite of recent watermarking models, including TrustMark, InvisMark, RoSteALS, HiDDeN, and WAM, demonstrating that adapted encoders closely reproduce target residuals and that adapted decoders recover messages with near-optimal accuracy under standard augmentations and distortions. We show that cross-model adaptation, with applications in interoperable and upgradable watermarking, can be achieved with as few as 1-2M trainable parameters per component (e.g., the 2M decoder adapter used in our multi-decoder inference pipeline).
papers.authors: Mehrdad Saberi, Vishal Asnani, Shruti Agarwal, Soheil Feizi, John Collomosse

papers.title: Homomorphic Encryption and Bootstrapping for Real Matrices over Conjugate-Invariant Rings
papers.abstract: The conjugate-invariant variant of CKKS (CI-CKKS) by Kim and Song encrypts real vectors over the subring of a power-of-two cyclotomic ring fixed by $X \mapsto X^{-1}$, with as many real slots as the rank of the ring. The Gentry–Lee scheme (GL) packs batches of complex matrices into a three-variable ring and multiplies them natively. GL bootstrapping replaces the rotations of the slot transforms with ciphertext–plaintext matrix products. We combine the two lines of work. First, we give a bootstrapping procedure for CI-CKKS: its transforms factor the real decoding matrix into sparse stages, and its modular reduction runs only once, on real slots, and needs no conjugation key. Second, by folding the three GL variables under their inversions, we obtain three subrings that have real slots and are closed under the matrix product; they define $\mathsf{CI}^{1}\text{-}\mathsf{GL}$, $\mathsf{CI}^{2}\text{-}\mathsf{GL}$, and $\mathsf{CI}^{3}\text{-}\mathsf{GL}$. We describe $\mathsf{CI}^{3}\text{-}\mathsf{GL}$ in detail: it encrypts real matrices, needs no conjugation, and, for the same matrix size and number of matrices, has keys of half the rank of GL keys. Third, we adapt the matrix-product bootstrapping of GL to $\mathsf{CI}^{3}\text{-}\mathsf{GL}$. We prototyped these techniques.
papers.authors: Ilaria Chillotti, Hyojun Kim, Yeongmin Lee, Yongwoo Lee, Damien Ligier

papers.title: Revisiting homomorphic AES evaluation with Hybrid Byte-Bit Packing
papers.abstract: Homomorphic AES evaluation is an important benchmark for practical FHE systems. Existing BGV-based AES transciphering schemes typically employ byte-oriented representations, which are well suited for exploiting the algebraic structure of the multiplicative inversion in the SubBytes operation. However, evaluating the affine transformation and subsequent linear layers in this representation introduces additional automorphisms and key-switching operations. In this work, we propose a hybrid byte-bit packing strategy for efficient BGV-based AES transciphering. After performing the multiplicative inversion in the SubBytes operation, we introduce an unpacking procedure to convert the slot packing scheme from byte-oriented to bit-oriented. The affine transformation in SubBytes and subsequent AES linear transformations are unified and evaluated over GF(2) using homomorphic additions, avoiding the key-switching operations involved in the packed byte-oriented evaluation of these linear components. We further optimize the unpacking procedure using a hoisting technique, achieving a 2.5× speedup in unpacking latency compared with the non-hoisted implementation. We implement our approach in HElib and evaluate it under parameters satisfying at least 128-bit security. Experimental results demonstrate per-block latency speedups of 2.6× and 11.7× without bootstrapping, and 2.1× and 3.3× with bootstrapping, on a local machine and a 64-thread server, respectively, compared with the reproduced BGV-based AES baseline under the same software, hardware, and security settings.
papers.authors: Lu Zhang, Xuan Shen, Ruida Wang, Xianhui Lu, Yin Zhang, Chao Li, Shaojing Fu

papers.title: VellSSLH: Sound Type-Guided Selective Speculative Load Hardening for LLVM IR
papers.abstract: Constant-time cryptographic programs written in C can still leak secrets during speculative execution. Mispredicted branches may allow instructions to access secret data and expose it through observable behavior. Speculative load hardening (SLH) addresses these leaks, but protecting values unnecessarily can introduce significant runtime overhead. We present VellSSLH, which selectively inserts speculative load hardening at LLVM IR. Programmers specify Public and Secret inputs in annotated C programs, and our analysis infers which values may become secret during speculation. The transformation then inserts misspeculation-flag operations and protections only where needed. VellSCT, our extracted checker, validates the resulting LLVM IR. We formalize speculative constant-time (SCT) security by extending Vellvm's LLVM semantics with speculative execution, attacker directives, and leakage observations. Our security type system reasons about SSA joins, symbolic values, poison, pointer provenance, and observable faults, and supports declared declassifications and trusted external services. In Rocq, we prove that programs accepted by the checker satisfy SCT, and that a reference hardening transformation preserves architectural behavior. Evaluated optimized variants are rechecked for SCT but are not covered by this preservation proof. Our mechanized guarantees apply at LLVM IR; security of the generated binary additionally depends on backend and hardware assumptions. We evaluate VellSSLH on 24 cryptographic entries on a bare-metal Intel processor. VellSSLH achieves 4.03% lower geometric-mean runtime than LLVM SLH, with 13 comparisons favoring VellSSLH, eight favoring LLVM SLH, and three inconclusive. For X25519, VellSSLH improves runtime by 22.69% over LLVM SLH with only 1.86% overhead over unprotected code. Compared with Ultimate SLH, VellSSLH achieves 19.65% lower runtime.
papers.authors: Swarn Priya

papers.title: DeCompCert: A Verified Decompiler for CompCert-Generated AArch64
papers.abstract: DeCompCert is a Rocq-verified decompiler for AArch64 assembly generated by CompCert. It reconstructs CompCert C through nine reverse passes, combining deductively verified transformations with translation validation. Untrusted OCaml and Datalog analyses propose candidate reconstructions, while verified validators accept only candidates that satisfy the required semantic correspondence. The composed correctness theorem guarantees that every defined, safe behavior of an accepted C reconstruction is matched by the input CompCert assembly; under a safety assumption, the two programs are observationally equivalent. We evaluate DeCompCert on approximately 2.16 million lines of C. With exact function and call signatures, it reconstructs and recompiles all 3,173 eligible contexts under both unoptimized and optimized CompCert pipelines. Without retained signatures, its cumulative inference portfolio validates 2,606 of 3,164 contexts (82.4%), while the platform-plus-IDA configuration validates 2,407 contexts (76.1%). Native execution and output-quality experiments further evaluate the generated C and characterize the remaining limitations in signature recovery and source resemblance.
papers.authors: Swarn Priya, Basavesh Ammanaghatta Shivakumar, Thomas Gilray, Kristopher Micinski

papers.title: Batch, Pack, and Prove: More Efficient Verifiable Computation for CKKS
papers.abstract: An important challenge in homomorphic encryption (HE) is ensuring the integrity of the encrypted computations. Although verifiable computation can address this in theory, making it practical is far from trivial. [Cascudo et al. CRYPTO 2025] recently proposed a solution to this problem for the CKKS scheme. In particular, they propose new succinct arguments that efficiently prove arithmetic circuits and range checks over the ring $R_q = \mathbb{Z}_q[Y]/(Y^N+1)$, and combine them to prove computations on CKKS ciphertexts. Despite the important progress, their work faces scalability challenges: the size of the polynomial commitment proofs, a large $O(N)$ overhead in range proofs, and the lack of an explicit method for efficient -- sublinear in circuit size -- verification. In this paper we present new techniques that remove all these bottlenecks. First, we provide a more efficient arithmetization of CKKS computations. Second, we introduce BatchFold, a new polynomial commitment for $R_q$ that supports batched evaluations and achieves shorter proofs. Third, we design packing, a novel algebraic technique that eliminates the need to commit to massive polynomials and removes the $O(N)$ overhead in range proofs. Finally, we introduce SparsePack, an efficient protocol for proving the evaluations of sparse, circuit-dependent polynomials, leveraging both packing and batched evaluations. We evaluate the efficiency of our solution on a generic neural network architecture, achieving proofs several orders of magnitude smaller and faster than prior approaches.
papers.authors: Ignacio Cascudo, Anamaria Costache, Daniele Cozzo, Dario Fiore, Antonio Guimarães, Eduardo Soria-Vazquez

papers.title: CANTraj: Recovering Vehicle Trajectories from CAN Signals in Naturalistic Driving
papers.abstract: Open driving releases and usage-based insurance programs often claim to prevent privacy breaches by omitting GPS records when sharing or collecting vehicle data. However, removing GPS coordinates from driving logs does not erase the location information carried by vehicle signals. While prior route-inference attacks have demonstrated that speed, steering, and driving events can be matched to road networks to reconstruct trajectories, existing studies rely on inconsistent prior assumptions and evaluation metrics and are tested only on small, restricted datasets, making their results difficult to compare and their real-world effectiveness uncertain. We release CANTraj, a naturalistic driving dataset pairing decoded CAN events with time-aligned GNSS trajectories (3,940 drives, 454 drivers), and CANTraj-Bench for evaluating trajectory recovery (3,675 drives, 431 drivers, 1,380 hours, 85,919 km). On 776 evaluation drives from 94 unseen drivers, we compare six re-implemented attacks and benchmark baselines under explicit information-access protocols, paired comparisons, and metrics incorporating failures. Experiments show that combining steering signals with road-network constraints yields the largest gain: With a known start and heading, adding steering to speed raises the online map filter's five-minute route recovery from 56% to 87%, with a median average displacement error of 43 m versus 921 m for map-free dead reckoning. Offline beam search recovers 88% of test routes with the heading and 81% without it. Because methods fail on different windows, we also evaluate an LLM harness that selects among candidate routes on 659 five-minute windows; its best configuration recovers 79% of routes on test and 83% on few-shot, outperforming the best baseline on test and matching it on few-shot. Data and code at huggingface.co/datasets/HenryYHW/CANTraj and github.com/WangYuHang-cmd/GPS--CAN.
papers.authors: Yuhang Wang, Jingxin Yang, Chuheng Wei, Suyang Chen, Haozhuang Chi, Hao Zhou

papers.title: Forget the Lineage: Forward-Secure, Lineage-Complete Cryptographic Erasure for LLM-Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents keep a long-term memory that the model itself writes: summaries, extracted facts and embeddings derived from what users said. Deleting a message is therefore not enough: its derivatives, storage residue and backups survive. We define lineage-complete forward-secure erasure: after a forget request, an adversary that later obtains all storage and the agent's current keys learns nothing about the forgotten input or any memory derived from it. We present LinEra, which encrypts each memory under a key derived from its parents' keys along the derivation graph; source keys come from a puncturable pseudorandom function, so forgetting is a single puncture and every descendant becomes unreadable without being located. A sound lineage rule records as parents everything the writer saw, which confines all influence of a source to its descendants. We prove security and lineage integrity and integrate LinEra with mem0. With real LLMs from two families (1.5B to 7B parameters) writing the memory of LoCoMo conversations, an attacker holding every file and the current keys recovers, on all ten conversations written by the largest model, 70 of 71 forgotten secrets after logical deletion, 67 with per-object or epoch keys, and none with LinEra; the same holds for every writer tested. The price is a larger forgetting radius, which follows a simple law in the writer's fan-in: forgetting 1% of turns erases 73.0% of derived memories with session-level summaries but only 3.8% with four-turn windows, which also answer better; re-deriving restores what is lost.
papers.authors: Yulliwas Ameur, Billal Mokhtari, Samia Bouzefrane

papers.title: Game-Theoretic Analysis of RIS-Assisted Challenge-Response PLA - Part II: Partial Channel Knowledge
papers.abstract: We consider a physical layer authentication scenario in which a legitimate user (Alice) communicates with an authenticator (Bob) through a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS), controlled by Bob. An attacker (Trudy) aims to impersonate Alice by suitably precoding her messages and still transmitting them through the RIS. This two-part study analyzes this attack-defense interaction between Bob and Trudy under perfect (Part I) and partial (Part II) channel knowledge by all the agents. Part I formulates the joint RIS selection and precoder design under perfect channel knowledge as a finite zero-sum game, establishing exact channel subspace conditions for attack indistinguishability alongside equilibrium mixed strategies. Part II extends the defense to incomplete channel information, where each agent observes only its own channel, by formulating a finite-action Bayesian game and characterizing the resulting Bayesian Nash equilibrium. Simulations in geometric and 3GPP TR 38.901 UMi-NLOS channels reveal that authentication performance is governed by available spatial degrees of freedom, channel correlation, and operating signal-to-noise ratio. The proposed equilibrium strategies effectively balance communication rate and security, outperforming conventional benchmark policies.
papers.authors: Anna V. Guglielmi, Linda Senigagliesi, Marco Baldi, Stefano Tomasin

papers.title: A Note on Non-interactive Deniable Secret Sharing from Indistinguishability Obfuscation
papers.abstract: Deniable secret sharing, introduced by Canetti et al. (TCC 2025), protects shareholders when a subset of them is coerced into revealing their shares. Namely, a set of fakers can produce fake shares that are consistent with a fake secret of their choice, and that are indistinguishable from real shares. Very recently, Amores et al. (TCC 2026) studied deniable secret sharing in a setting where the fakers cannot interact to produce their fake shares. Specifically, each faker locally computes its fake share given only its own share, the set of fakers, and the fake secret. Their constructions of non-interactive deniable secret sharing either have shares of exponential size or rely on virtual black-box obfuscation. We show how to upgrade any secret sharing scheme, for any access structure, into a non-interactive deniable secret sharing scheme using a collusion-resistant constrained PRF with static security, which can be instantiated from polynomially-secure indistinguishability obfuscation and one-way functions. Our transformation incurs an additive share size overhead that is polynomial in the number of shareholders. By using indistinguishability obfuscation directly, together with a somewhere-statistically binding hash, we further reduce the overhead to polylogarithmic in the number of shareholders. In combination with prior work on succinct computational secret sharing, we get succinct deniable secret sharing from indistinguishability obfuscation and standard assumptions.
papers.authors: Shafik Nassar

papers.title: Early-Stopping Dishonest Majority Broadcast with Optimal Round Complexity
papers.abstract: Early-stopping broadcast protocols guarantee termination as a function of the number $f\le t$ of parties actually corrupted in an execution, rather than of the worst-case bound $t<n$. Loss and Nielsen (Eurocrypt 2024) gave such a protocol for every $t<n$, terminating within $O(\min\{f^2+1,t+1\})$ rounds, with polynomial communication and from a plain public-key infrastructure (PKI). In the other direction, Choi, Choi, Liu, and Zikas (ePrint 2026/1878) recently proved a stopping lower bound which implies that $f+3$ rounds are necessary whenever $n+f<2\min\{t,n-2\}$, a condition that covers a broad part of the dishonest-majority regime. It has remained open whether this bound can be attained, even at the cost of exponential communication. In this work, we present a deterministic early-stopping broadcast protocol in which every honest party outputs and terminates within $\min\{f+3,t+1\}$ rounds for every $t<n$. The protocol is built from exponential information gathering (EIG) graphs and incurs exponential communication. It works in the plain PKI model with idealized signatures and is secure against a strongly adaptive adversary. Its stopping round complexity is therefore optimal throughout the stated range of the lower bound.
papers.authors: Renas Bacho, Kecheng Shi

papers.title: Deterministic ECDSA on secp256k1: the RFC 6979 assumption, a counterexample, and the state of deployed implementations
papers.abstract: RFC 6979 derives the ECDSA nonce as $k = F_x(h)$, with $F_x$ HMAC_DRBG keyed by the signing key x. We isolate the assumption its security rests on, A*: at known public key $Q = xG$, the signing transcript under nonces $F_x()$ is indistinguishable from the transcript under uniform nonces. A* suffices, and it is neither PRF security of HMAC nor auxiliary-input PRF security (AI-PRF) of $F_x$. A function $F'(x, h) = P_{Ext(xG)}(h)$ is a PRF under standard assumptions yet leaks x from one signature; the same holds for unmodified RFC 6979 over a compression function that keeps the PRF and dual-PRF properties used in proofs of HMAC, given a collision-resistance premise. A* and AI-PRF are separated in both directions. A* does not imply AI-PRF if the one-bit hidden number problem is hard. Conversely, in the standard model: any AI-PRF can be modified so that it stays one while two chosen-digest signing queries reveal x; under DDH with one public random point, or decisional square Diffie-Hellman without it, there is an AI-PRF whose key is recovered from signatures on two ordinary hashed messages; and a third function, under PRF security and DLP, violates A* while the scheme stays unforgeable. With an ideal compression function, A* follows tightly from DLP in the presence of a randomized-ECDSA signing oracle, and a nonce key independent of x removes the assumption. The secret HMAC message block is $2^{-127.65}$ from uniform on secp256k1, $2^{-32}$ on P-256 and 0.336 on brainpoolP256r1. An audit of 31 secp256k1 implementations finds that 28 sign deterministically without added entropy and that the raw-message deviation from bits2octets of libsecp256k1 before 0.2.0 survives in NBitcoin, dcrd and btcec v2. Low-R grinding needs no assumption beyond A*, and every nonzero Fourier coefficient of the low-R nonce set is below $2^{-116.9}$ unconditionally. We give test vectors for the untested $h >= n$ branch
papers.authors: Ilia Prosianoi

papers.title: RuralShield: Super Intelligence-Assisted Security Triage and Serverless Infrastructure for Resource-Constrained Healthcare
papers.abstract: Resource-constrained healthcare providers must connect cloud security controls to an operational response process. Introducing language-model assessments adds an authorization problem: a recommendation must be converted into a permitted action against a specific resource. RuralShield combines a configurable serverless application foundation with structured model assessment, deterministic routing, and human-approved containment. Its design separates workload access, assessment validation, and action authorization so that each boundary produces inspectable records. We evaluate the implementation through a frozen 120-hour non-AI workload and separate desktop and AWS AI cohorts. The workload recorded 999,861 authenticated requests and 999,860 successful responses, with one HTTP 404 and one missing minute representing 139 scheduled requests. Median, 95th-percentile, and 99th-percentile Ohio client latencies were 28.57, 53.01, and 110.77 ms. Eight successful model requests exercised assessment and reporting in two four-case cohorts. The AWS cohort and five scripted controls produced nine completed workflows, including two human-approved Lambda containment cases with verified restoration of the original concurrency setting. Source-linked, checksum-verified archives preserved the records before scoped cleanup. The study demonstrates an inspectable integration of application controls and human-mediated AI response under the evaluated synthetic conditions.
papers.authors: Mohammad Arman Ullah, Asif Ahmed

papers.title: Securing Multi-Agent Systems by Design
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems solve complex tasks by decomposing them into subtasks, delegating the subtasks to agents, and aggregating the agents' responses using an aggregation rule. Malicious agents can manipulate the final solution by providing malicious responses to their assigned subtasks. In this paper, we first propose response manipulation attacks (ReMA), which iteratively optimize malicious responses to maximize attack effectiveness. Specifically, we formulate untargeted and targeted attacks as optimization problems and develop an approach to approximately solve these problems by iteratively refining malicious responses based on feedback from a surrogate multi-agent system. To defend against such attacks, we further propose SecMAS, a secure aggregation rule that leverages the semantic similarities among agent responses to select the response that is most consistent with a sufficiently large subset of the other responses. We theoretically establish security guarantees for SecMAS against both untargeted and targeted attacks. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that existing aggregation rules are vulnerable to ReMA, whereas SecMAS effectively defends against all evaluated attacks, including adaptive variants of ReMA, while maintaining utility comparable to that of existing aggregation rules.
papers.authors: Xilong Wang, Xiaoxing Chen, Neil Gong

papers.title: Evaluating the Robustness of PRNU Source-Camera Attribution to the Fingerprint-Copy Attack: An Open Toolkit with Triangle-Test Detection
papers.abstract: Photo-Response Non-Uniformity (PRNU) is the de facto standard trace for sensor-level source-camera attribution, and a high Peak-to-Correlation-Energy (PCE) between a questioned image and a camera reference fingerprint is routinely treated as strong evidence of common origin. The fingerprint-copy attack of Goljan, Fridrich and Chen (2011) shows that this signal can be forged: an adversary who estimates a target camera's fingerprint from that camera's publicly available images can inject a scaled copy of it into an unrelated photograph, producing a forgery that clears a PCE decision threshold despite never having been taken by the target device. We present prnucf, an open, auditable toolkit that pairs a reference implementation of the (additive) fingerprint-copy attack with the triangle-test detector and a cohort-calibrated decision procedure, so that practitioners can quantify how fragile a PRNU attribution is against this attack on their own pipelines. On a controlled multi-camera Monte-Carlo benchmark the attack reaches an arbitrary target PCE at a mean PSNR of 59.2 dB (visually lossless), yet the triangle test separates forgeries from innocent images with an area under the ROC curve of 0.999, detecting every forgery at a cohort-calibrated 5% false-positive operating point. We discuss why a fixed significance cut-off is not safe in casework, the limitations of synthetic validation, and the open problem of extending explainable detection to the modern, GAN-based generation of fingerprint-transfer attacks. The toolkit is released under the MIT license with an explicit dual-use statement.
papers.authors: Zeno J. M. H. Geradts

papers.title: RRHL: A Relational Logic for Rényi Differential Privacy of Private Learning
papers.abstract: Differential privacy is the standard framework for defining privacy-preserving computation and is adopted in large-scale production systems, including industrial-level private learning. The underlying algorithms are based on complex privacy-enhancing mechanisms such as privacy amplification by subsampling and correlated noising. Proving their privacy requires advanced reasoning techniques such as the moments accountant and shifted composition; no existing approach to formal verification supports all of them. In this work, we introduce RRHL: a relational program logic for proving Rényi differential privacy of imperative programs with continuous sampling instructions. Its judgments express bounds on the privacy budgets of instructions as functions of the program states, and its composition of budgets is sharp. We use RRHL to prove differential privacy of the algorithms widely implemented and deployed. These include several variants of DP-SGD and DP-FTRL, and gradient descent with per-record Rényi filters. In several cases the bounds match the best known Rényi differential privacy analyses. The logic, its soundness proof and the case studies are formalized in Lean. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first formal privacy analysis, via a relational program logic, of private learning algorithms with state-of-the-art Rényi differential privacy bounds.
papers.authors: Gilles Barthe, Davide Davoli

papers.title: Can LLMs Write Backdoors? An Empirical Security Study of Weight-Space Programming
papers.abstract: Recent advances in weight-space programming (WSP) have demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) can directly inspect and modify neural network weights without conventional gradient-based training. While this capability opens new possibilities for model improvement, it also raises an important security question: Can LLMs exploit weight-space programming to inject backdoors into neural networks? To answer this question, we present an empirical security study of LLM-driven weight-space programming for backdoor injection. Specifically, we investigate whether general-purpose LLMs can directly modify the weights of target models according to natural-language instructions, without accessing task-specific data, performing forward passes, or computing gradients. We evaluate five LLMs as weight editors across three target architectures: an MLP on MNIST, ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, and Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on AG News. Our experiments reveal three key findings. First, LLM-driven weight editing can successfully inject backdoors across different architectures while largely preserving clean performance. Second, successful attacks can require remarkably few parameter modifications, including only six parameters for the MLP and 0.02% of the weights for a fine-tuned Qwen model. Third, editing capabilities vary substantially across LLMs and target architectures: although all five LLMs successfully backdoor the MLP, only GPT-6 Astra succeeds across all three targets. These findings highlight an emerging security risk of weight-space programming and underscore the importance of safeguarding LLM-driven weight editing.
papers.authors: Zhaojia Wang, Jiucui Lu, Zheng Li

papers.title: Quadratic APN Functions of $\mathbb{F}_2^{10}$ with a Self-Equivalence of Prime Order
papers.abstract: Almost perfect nonlinear (APN) functions of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ have the lowest possible differential uniformity. The only known APN permutation in even dimension, in dimension six, is equivalent to a quadratic APN function with a nontrivial linear self-equivalence; no APN permutation is known for even $n \geq 8$. In a published collection of about 3.8 million quadratic APN classes of dimension eight, at most 0.34% have a nontrivial linear self-equivalence. In dimension ten, the 25 literature classes considered here all have one. We study all quadratic APN functions of $\mathbb{F}_2^{10}$ with such a self-equivalence, which usually confines them to a much smaller linear space. Up to conjugacy and power similarity, self-equivalences of prime order have 299 types. We settle 298 of them. Elementary lemmas exclude 280 types, and exhaustive searches confirm this for 242 of them. The other 18 types are settled by exhaustive searches with exact equivalence certificates. Up to extended affine equivalence, the 298 types contain 29 classes of quadratic APN functions, four of them new. This also classifies the quadratic APN functions with coefficients in a subfield. Exactly 24 classes contain one with coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_4$, and all 3 that contain one with coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_{32}$ are among them. The open type consists of the quadratic canonical triplicate functions. They correspond to maximum additive Hermitian rank-distance codes. Three different searches find only the invariants of 16 classes, all among the 29. We conjecture there are no others. No quadratic APN function in the 298 settled types is Carlet-Charpin-Zinoviev equivalent to a permutation.
papers.authors: Emanuele Bellini

papers.title: On the Same Track: Privacy Leaks in Electric Rail Transport via Magnetic Fields
papers.abstract: Inertial sensors of smartphones are a well-known privacy risk, as they allow inferring sensitive user movements and activity without explicit permissions. Among these sensors, the magnetometer has received little attention, as it is assumed to measure mainly the Earth's magnetic field. In this paper, we show that electric trains generate distinctive magnetic fields that can be captured by a smartphone magnetometer. Apps deployed on the device can access these signals without user permission, enabling two novel attacks on passenger privacy: First, we are able to determine whether the user is riding an electric train (transport mode detection). Second, we can infer whether other victims are aboard the same train due to shared patterns in the magnetic field (colocation prediction). In an empirical evaluation across 217 train rides, we demonstrate that both attacks are effective, confirming a real-world threat. We discuss countermeasures and argue that magnetometer access should require explicit user permission in mobile operating systems.
papers.authors: Stefan Czybik, Pia Hanfeld, Konrad Rieck

papers.title: PrivacyPR: A Dataset of Real-World Privacy Fixes for Benchmarking Privacy-Aware Code Review
papers.abstract: Coding agents increasingly review code, yet whether they catch the privacy defects that laws such as the GDPR require software to avoid remains largely untested, partly because few datasets connect real privacy defects to their accepted fixes and review context. We present PrivacyPR, a dataset of 4,131 merged GitHub pull requests (PRs) from 1,469 repositories, created between June 2018 and January 2024. Each PR includes its commits, diffs, review discussion, and LLM-generated labels for privacy relevance, fix type, and GDPR principles. PrivacyPR provides 1,169 high-confidence privacy fixes and 1,643 non-fix PRs, together with Verified, a manually checked split of 250 privacy fixes and 250 non-fix PRs, and Small, a 100 + 100 subset for evaluation. On Verified, both annotators endorsed 72% of the LLM's GDPR-principle assignments. Beyond supporting empirical study of how privacy defects arise and are fixed, PrivacyPR provides a benchmark for privacy-aware code review on real, developer-accepted fixes. Its evaluation harness reverts each fix to reintroduce the defect. On Small, two coding agents detect only 42-51% of defects under a generic review prompt, but 88-91% when explicitly asked to check privacy, while flagging 11-15% of non-fix PRs. These results show that privacy defects can be detected by coding agents, but that detection depends strongly on review intent and comes with false alarms. Data, code, reviews, judge verdicts, and an extensible evaluation harness are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23744765.
papers.authors: Hua Yang, Aditya Bhardwaj, Shidong Pan, Bowen Xu

papers.title: From Bytes to Behavior: Request-Level Attribution from Live GPU Hidden States
papers.abstract: Existing memory forensics for machine learning systems typically targets static artifacts, such as model weights or prompt logs, rather than the transient computational states of a live inference process. This gap limits an examiner's ability to analyze the specific behavior of a running large language model (LLM) service that cannot be restarted or modified. We present a method for acquiring per-layer residual-stream activations from a live GPU process using a non-modifying debugger, without requiring prior knowledge of the model's architecture parameters or weights. The approach employs a general six-stage process with platform-specific adapters, utilizing either a PyTorch allocator clock or a kernel-launch clock to identify and read tensor allocations from video memory. We validate this acquisition on 33 open-source decoder-only models across nine architecture classes, demonstrating that the recovered bytes are byte-exact and usable for downstream analysis. As a use case, we apply linear probes trained on standard framework activations to the recovered states, successfully distinguishing refusal from compliance with an AUROC of 0.88 on held-out prompts. This work establishes that live, observational access to intermediate hidden states is feasible on named inference platforms, providing a new source of evidence for examining the operational behavior of deployed AI systems.
papers.authors: Jonathan Pan, Yidi Yuan, Xin Wei Chia, Xinhui Su, Vincent Tan, Brenda Ong

papers.title: Hello Again: Exploiting Replay Protected Monotonic Counters to Brute-Force Windows Hello PINs
papers.abstract: Windows Hello is the primary authentication mechanism on over one billion Windows 11 devices, supporting PINs as short as four digits. Such low-entropy PINs are viable only because the TPM's anti-hammering protection mitigates brute-force attacks. Most modern x86 platforms rely on firmware TPMs (fTPMs) that persist their non-volatile (NV) state, including the lockout state, to SPI flash. On newer platforms, rollback prevention of this state is delegated to the flash chip via Replay Protected Monotonic Counters (RPMCs), a JEDEC-standardized mechanism operating over a physically accessible bus. We present the first practical security analysis of RPMC in shipping x86 systems. Using low-cost interposer hardware, we identify multiple implementation flaws, two of which fundamentally undermine RPMC's security model: First, Winbond SPI flash - the leading NOR flash vendor with over 25% market share - leaks its HMAC key under voltage glitching, enabling arbitrary counter forgery. Second, AMD's NV controller does not verify RPMC increments, so an interposer can suppress them unnoticed. Moreover, AMD platforms without RPMC flash appear to lack NV rollback protection altogether: on two AMD desktops, reflashing an old image resets the fTPM's lockout counters. Both flaws enable rollbacks of the fTPM's NV state (AMD, Intel, or Pluton), including its lockout counters. We demonstrate this end-to-end on locked, encrypted hardware: our setup finds a 4-digit Windows Hello PIN in 40 hours instead of 69 days. A compromised PIN also grants access to device-bound keys and Hello-based enterprise SSO. The same primitive defeats BitLocker's TPM+PIN pre-boot protector, reducing the worst-case time for a default-length 6-digit PIN from 19 years to 20 days.
papers.authors: Christian Werling, Matti Finder, Hans Niklas Jacob, Julian Prein, Niclas Kühnapfel, Jean-Pierre Seifert

papers.title: Beyond Bot Labels: Retrospective Consequence-Grounded Ranking of Attributed Cache Harm in E-Commerce Logs
papers.abstract: Web caches reduce origin load and latency, but automated traffic can either warm them or evict objects shoppers reuse, lowering the cache hit ratio (CHR). Existing bot defenses generally infer automation from User-Agent (UA) strings or behavior rather than identify sessions that impose cross-session cache harm. We instead formulate the task as ranking sessions by eviction damage and propose consequence-grounded session ranking. A single chronological replay attributes each eviction-induced miss by a protected shopping session (a victim) to the session whose insertion last evicted the object. A behavioral model predicts the target from session behavior alone. Selected sessions bypass the cache but remain origin-served. In a controlled check of 539 non-victim sessions selected across harm levels, attribution order tracks victim-hit changes after removal (Spearman correlation 0.80). On a 12.7-million-request real trace, the top 1% of sessions carry 48.8% of attributed harm. Sessions without bot tags contribute 49.1% of this tier's harm. At the 20% request-volume target, the default conditional CHR difference reaches 93% of the UA baseline, which selects 47 times as many sessions. Six training seeds show little variation. This comparison conditions on the victims that remain, so we also report victim bypass. Local replay and retraining on a second store reproduce harm concentration and a top tier dominated by sessions without bot tags. These results establish attributed cross-session harm as an outcome-based target for retrospective cache audits and selective intervention design.
papers.authors: Jisoo Kim, Youngwoo Seo, Seonghoon Jeong

papers.title: Condensing Law of Security Information
papers.abstract: Scaling laws indicate that the generalization error of a large language model (LLM) decreases monotonically with model size once data is sufficient, and the corollary that larger models outperform smaller ones is now widely accepted. We argue that this corollary fails in security: decisions there hinge on anomalous inputs, which are long-tailed (e.g., zero-day attacks) and therefore poorly served by likelihood fitting. Worse still, the capability brought about by scale (e.g., inferring the intended whole from a corrupted part) leads a LLM silently \emph{repair} the anomaly before any downstream security head ever sees it. We formalize this as a tradeoff between two quantities: the cognitive capability $K(W)=I(W;P)$ that a model holds about the world distribution, and the security-information retention $R(W)=\frac{I(Z;S)}{I(A;S)}$ that survives in its intermediate representation. We derive three information-theoretic bounds to connect them: an upper bound on restoration accuracy in terms of $K(W)$, an upper bound on $R(W)$ in terms of the restoration error, and a Fano lower bound on security-task error in terms of $R(W)$. These theorems approximately imply that usable security information is a product of how much security information survives and how well it can be extracted, indicating that optimal usable security information can be achieved at a certain model size. We state this as the \emph{condensing law of security information}: usable security information is unimodal in model size, so security generalization error is U-shaped and is minimized at a finite $N^{\star}$ rather than decreasing without bound. The experiments on various real-world LLMs validate the condensing law, indicating that there is an optimal model size to solve security issues.
papers.authors: Qi Tan, Tianyu Cui, Qi Li, Ke Xu

papers.title: Inferring Sensitive Events in Multi-Mode Cyber-Physical Systems via Scheduling Side Channels
papers.abstract: Many cyber-physical systems (CPS) are multi-mode: they switch between operating modes with different tasksets and timing parameters in response to physical events or user activity. We show that these mode changes create a timing side channel: by altering the interference experienced by co-running tasks, they let an unprivileged co-resident observer infer sensitive events, such as a homeowner's arrival or a vehicle's route, from its own execution timing and, on multicore platforms, its core assignment. Existing schedule-based attacks and defenses miss this channel because they assume single-mode systems or target a specific, known victim task. We present STAMP, a lightweight attack that needs no knowledge of task parameters or scheduling policy, and works whether or not the system exposes its modes. On a ZoneMinder home-security deployment, STAMP identifies the modes with 94.7% accuracy on unseen hardware, using under 0.5% of one core. On ROS 2 AMCL with the Oxford RobotCar dataset, it identifies which of seven route segments a vehicle traversed with 86.0% accuracy on unseen platforms. A schedule-randomization defense lowers detection recall to 0.53, at which setting only 53.9% as many jobs finish on time. At higher noise ($ε=10$), on-time job completion reduces to 14.4%, while introducing new leakage in 14.1% of the tasksets.
papers.authors: Yifan Cai, Linh Thi Xuan Phan

papers.title: Round-Key Equivalence and Collisions of the Revised MoFang
papers.abstract: The revised reference implementation of MoFang moves the S-box of the second message half to row 1, which does not eliminate the original per-round key cancellation. Collisions of this type on the original version have been independently reported2,3; this paper does not repeat those findings, and instead proves for the revised version that when the nonzero words of that half are confined to three designated positions, the full message expansion preserves the per-round cancellation, so that every input has 16 round-key-equivalent inputs. The property holds for any common chaining value and transfers to the complete behavior of the six reference variants under full padding, fixed initialization, and XOF output interfaces. Furthermore, the sufficient condition is promoted to a complete classification of the round key map: the common difference of any two equivalent inputs must belong to the original 16 period-two masks, and the equivalence class sizes can only be 1, 2, 4, or 16, with size 16 corresponding exactly to the original domain D0. For the DM variants, necessary and sufficient conditions for all nontrivial equivalence classes are given, together with an exact integer count of the covered domain (log2 ≈ 814.04647); the domain covered by equivalence classes of size at least four admits a three-state matrix counting formula. These results char acterize the equivalence of complete round-key sequences; the domain sizes do not indicate running time or security strength. The object of study is fixed to the 64-bit word model corresponding to the public submission; mathematical proofs, computer-assisted counting, and experimental verification against the reference C code are stated separately.
papers.authors: Zhang zhihong, Liu fengyaxuan

papers.title: Representational Geometry as a Diagnostic for Adversarial Robustness
papers.abstract: Adversarial training is a common technique for making neural networks more robust to small, intentionally crafted input perturbations, and robustness is commonly measured through accuracy under attack. By exploring inter-network representations across different adversarial training objectives, we can analyze whether multiple networks organize their latent representations similarly. We study Multilayer Perceptrons trained on MNIST under three adversarial training regimes and compare the resulting population training dynamics and geometry to those of a vanilla network. We use M-PHATE to embed data samples across training epochs and examine how the geometry of the data changes during training under adversarial objectives. On penultimate-layer representations we measure displacement between clean and perturbed points, distributional distance through maximum mean discrepancy, and nearest-neighbor recovery. Our visualizations and quantitative analyses show that adversarial training leads to structural changes in how networks organize internal data representations, and robust accuracy and representational stability can rank the same defenses in opposite ways. These findings support a discussion of re-evaluating how practitioners approach the auditing of model robustness by treating latent representations and their training trajectories as diagnostic artifacts across sets of networks.
papers.authors: Brandon Ismalej, Alex Cloninger, Gal Mishne

papers.title: Binarization as an Attack Surface in Weightless Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Weightless Neural Networks (WNNs) are lightweight classifiers that binarize their inputs and learn by storing binary patterns in lookup memories, which makes them attractive for resource-constrained tasks such as intrusion detection. Because a small perturbation that crosses no binarization threshold leaves the binary input unchanged, WNNs may appear naturally robust to adversarial examples; a perturbation that does cross a threshold, however, can still change the prediction. We study this tension in WiSARD, the canonical RAM-based WNN, and in two variants that replace its memories with Bloom filters, Bloom WiSARD and BTHOWeN. A continuous perturbation reaches these classifiers only by crossing an encoding threshold, changing at least one binary tuple, and redirecting a memory query; we formalize this mechanism with a threshold-crossing bound and a response-margin certificate for standard Boolean WiSARD. Controlled MNIST experiments compare linear and data-driven thermometer encodings under model-agnostic sensitivity probes, a score-based Simulated Annealing attack, and surrogate-transfer attacks. Changing only the encoding while keeping each model otherwise fixed shows that encoding granularity can trade a small clean-accuracy loss for a large decrease in attack success. On the Bot-IoT, CICIDS, and UNSW-NB15 intrusion-detection datasets, adversarial perturbations lead WNN detectors to classify many attacks as normal traffic and to raise false alarms, even when their aggregate accuracy remains high.
papers.authors: Lucas Senos Coutinho, Matheus Vargas, Pedro Teixeira, Heudson Tosta Mirandola, Ori Rottenstreich, Priscila Machado Vieira Lima, Leandro Santiago, Daniel Sadoc Menasche

papers.title: Tractable Importance Sampling for Monte Carlo Privacy Accounting
papers.abstract: Evaluating tight Differential Privacy (DP) parameters for DP matrix factorization with privacy amplification by sampling requires analyzing high-dimensional, correlated Gaussian mixtures. Because integrating these mixture distributions to find the exact privacy failure probability ($δ$) is analytically intractable, these mechanisms are typically analyzed using Monte Carlo accounting. However, standard sampling suffers from prohibitive variance when estimating small $δ$ associated with strict privacy guarantees, which in turn requires a large sample complexity, making Monte Carlo accounting inefficient. We demonstrate that Monte Carlo accounting can be made much more efficient via importance sampling. We give a shifted importance sampling proposal distribution parameterized by a stretch factor $α> 1$. We prove a closed-form bound $B(α) < 1$ on the support of the importance-weighted estimator that holds identically for both directions of the hockey-stick divergence, show that $B$ is log-convex so that the optimal $α$ is a one-dimensional root-finding problem, and show that the resulting estimator seamlessly plugs into the KL-Hoeffding verification protocol used by past work, with a sample complexity reduced by exactly a factor of $1/B(α^*)$.
papers.authors: Galen Andrew, Arun Ganesh

papers.title: Online Allocation with Differential Privacy
papers.abstract: We study private online allocation problems, where allocation decisions must satisfy differential privacy (DP) to protect sensitive user information while optimizing performance under limited resources. We first formalize differential privacy notions suited to different privacy requirements in online allocation and establish the fundamental performance limits of any algorithm under these definitions. Based on these insights, we propose PPOA, a privacy-preserving meta algorithm for online allocation, and establish sufficient conditions under which PPOA preserves Joint DP (JDP) or Local DP (LDP) while achieving asymptotically near-optimal performance. Building on these conditions, PPOA can be instantiated into a variety of concrete algorithms. In particular, we present the specific designs, which include PPOA-DMD that preserves JDP and LDP and PPOA-FTRL that preserves JDP. We analyze their performance under both adversarial and stochastic settings and characterize the fundamental trade-offs between DP and allocation performance. Finally, we demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed algorithms via numerical experiments on AI model routing in battery-powered edge systems.
papers.authors: Jianyi Yang, Xingyu Zhou, Mostafa Mushsharat, Shaolei Ren

papers.title: I2C-GRPO: Insight Importance Checklist for Reinforcement Learning in a Multi-Agent DDoS Alert Triage Workflow
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for investigative tasks over incomplete evidence, such as cybersecurity alert triage, but reinforcement learning (RL) for such tasks is difficult: intermediate steps have no verifiable labels, rollouts are costly, and outcome rewards are sparse. We propose Insight Importance Checklist (I2C)-GRPO, a checklist reward for intermediate investigation steps. For each decision point, a panel of expert LLMs proposes investigative actions, their atomic forensic insights are extracted, and a separate three-model ranker panel orders the insights by importance. A reward model checks which ranked insights a candidate action targets and returns their consensus-weighted coverage. Because actions are scored without being executed, the reward is a proxy for expected investigative value, and training reduces to a one-step contextual bandit over fixed investigation prefixes. From a soft-computing perspective, the reward is an additive fuzzy measure whose rank-exponent weights act as an ordered weighted averaging (OWA)-type operator; one exponent sets its orness, i.e., how strongly the reward concentrates on the top of the judges' consensus. We train an open-weight Qwen3-4B Triage Agent within a fixed multi-agent Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) alert-triage workflow on DARPA 2000 LLDOS 1.0 and test it on an independent CSE-CIC-IDS2018 DDoS trace. Across three training seeds, the agent reaches a mean F1-score of 0.869, 5.9 and 9.7 points above uniform insight weights and DIVA, and a false-positive rate of 4.9% versus 16.4% for GPT-5-mini. Within the weighting family, false positives fall only at the highest-orness weighting evaluated. All claims are limited to DDoS alert triage; the code, task contexts, and ranked insight dataset will be released.
papers.authors: Eyal Zloof, Shaun Shuster, Aviram Zilberman, Chen Frydman, Inderjeet Singh, Andrés Murilo, Asaf Shabtai, Yuval Elovici, Rami Puzis

papers.title: Beyond Attack-Based Accuracy: Rethinking Adversarial Robustness Evaluation Through Structural Gradient Alignment
papers.abstract: Visual adversarial robustness remains a fundamental security property as vision systems evolve from conventional classifiers to vision-language models (VLMs) and large vision-language models (LVLMs), with visual inputs remaining an attack surface across generations. Yet existing evaluation methods often depend on prescribed attacks, in-distribution data, extensive probing, or classifier-specific formulations, limiting external auditing of diverse models. We introduce Structural Gradient Alignment (SGA), a complementary robustness metric measuring the structural alignment between input content and objective-conditioned local model sensitivity. SGA uses a few randomly sampled, unlabeled public probes that need not follow the downstream task distribution and only one input-gradient computation per model--probe pair. Across 38 distinct DNNs, VLMs, and LVLMs, SGA produces rankings consistent with attack-based references. Without robustness references, uncalibrated SGA achieves $83.72\%$ average pairwise agreement across eight public-probe conditions, outperforming the strongest overall baseline in all eight by $9.38$ percentage points on average. With known robustness orders of anchor models, calibrated SGA increases agreement to $85.36\%$. These results demonstrate an attack-agnostic, computationally efficient robustness signal across conventional DNNs, VLMs, and autoregressive LVLMs, downstream tasks, threat norms, probe distributions, and evaluator-knowledge settings. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/azrealwang/SGA.
papers.authors: Hanrui Wang, Yu Luo, Shuo Wang, Xingbo Dong, Zhe Jin, Isao Echizen

papers.title: iGRAIL: Blockchain-Based Generative Federated Learning for Trustworthy Healthcare Intelligence
papers.abstract: Healthcare organizations collect huge amounts of patient data from clinical records, medical tests, monitoring systems, and healthcare services. Such data can underpin intelligent healthcare analytics but remains distributed across institutions and cannot be shared directly due to privacy, security, and trust concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative learning without sharing raw patient records, but the exchanged model information remains vulnerable to privacy leakage, tampering, replay, and unauthorized access. In this paper, we propose iGRAIL, a blockchain-enabled generative FL framework for trustworthy healthcare intelligence. iGRAIL combines local generative learning for data augmentation with differential privacy to protect sensitive information during local training. Model communication is secured using cryptographic mechanisms, and blockchain-based verification and smart-contract access control ensure that only authorized, authentic, fresh, and integrity-preserving updates are accepted for federated aggregation. The framework is evaluated on four healthcare datasets and compared with the conventional FL and blockchain-based FL (BC-FL) under predictive, privacy, non-IID, scalability, malicious-update, security-verification, and runtime settings. For the two large diabetes datasets, iGRAIL improves accuracy by about 5.4-5.6%, the F1-score by 14.6-16.9%, and MCC by 16.0-18.1% over the best FL or BC-FL baseline. Increasing the strength of differential privacy reduces the privacy-loss parameter $ε$ by about 72.5% for the cancer dataset and 87.5% for the diabetes dataset, with only a limited loss in prediction performance. These results indicate that iGRAIL supports secure and scalable federated computing while preserving privacy, model integrity, and controlled participation, at the cost of additional computational overhead.
papers.authors: Debashis Das, Sourav Banerjee, Saraju P. Mohanty

papers.title: Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion
papers.abstract: Monitoring maritime activities is important for safety and security, particularly for detecting illegal activities, but remains challenging due to the size and complexity of the maritime domain. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is commonly used for this purpose, despite its known vulnerabilities. In contrast, space-based radio frequency (RF) observations provide an independent source of vessel activity but lack ship identification and therefore cannot identify vessels on their own. Following the CRISP-DM process, this study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to align individual RF detections with AIS trajectories, using temporal and spatial information while modeling noise and timing discrepancies. We evaluate it on NOAA AIS data with synthetic RF detections against nearest-neighbor baselines and analyze its errors with bias tests on trajectory length, sampling density, stationarity and AIS--RF distance. The length-corrected Forward score reaches a top-1 precision of $0.7776$ on the validation split of multi-candidate detections, where errors are possible, and an AUC of $0.637$ for detecting dark vessels among the detections that pass the prefilter. With a single RF detection, the score mostly reflects the AIS trajectory itself, and its errors favor longer and more stationary trajectories. A log-odds score, which compares the full model with a null model without match transitions, raises precision to $0.8580$ and AUC to $0.852$. Its length-corrected variant no longer shows a significant bias towards stationary trajectories and short inter-message distances, but still favors candidates farther from the RF detection. A time-weighted nearest-neighbor baseline without fitting remains ahead (precision $0.9013$, AUC $0.904$), so this single-detection, hand-designed PHMM formulation approaches but does not beat it.
papers.authors: Daniel Grimm, Kyra Jongman, Renato Cordeiro Ferreira, Giuseppe Cascavilla, Alfredo Cuzzocrea, Willem-Jan Van Den Heuvel

papers.title: Evolutionary-based Transfer Learning for Physical Attack on End-to-End Autoencoder Communications
papers.abstract: End-to-end autoencoder communication has emerged as a promising means of achieving efficient data transmission across various domains. Nevertheless, vulnerabilities have recently been revealed in these systems by adversarial attacks, wherein malevolent entities manipulate the transmitted signals to deceive the autoencoder. This paper leverages the applications of evolutionary algorithms to solve a challenging optimization problem of launching physical attacks against end-to-end autoencoder communication. For white-box scenarios, we introduce PAGA (Physical Attack based on Genetic Algorithm), which combines a genetic algorithm with elite population initialization to craft attack signals that degrade autoencoder performance. To gauge the efficacy of these attack signals, we employ a fitness function that assesses their capacity to induce substantial reconstruction errors and misclassification rates. A Multi-Factorial version of PAGA, referred to as PAMFGA, is proposed to deal with practical scenarios where the attackers have limited knowledge about the receiver, also known as a black-box attack. Our experimental results show that the proposed attacks can substantially degrade the reliability of the considered autoencoder communication systems across the evaluated settings. This study also underscores the critical importance of incorporating security considerations into the design and implementation of end-to-end autoencoder communication systems.
papers.authors: Ho Viet Duc Luong, Lang Hong Nguyet Anh, Huynh Thi Thanh Binh, Trinh Van Chien

papers.title: LLMs are Vulnerable to Malicious Requests with Indistinguishable Intent
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks can circumvent the safety mechanisms of Large Language Models (LLMs) and lead to the generation of harmful or policy-violating content. We first examine eight jailbreak methods against an LLM-based filter and observe that requests resembling normal user queries tend to have higher filter pass rates than those containing obvious anomalous patterns. This observation motivates the hypothesis that resemblance to normal requests may contribute to jailbreak success. We introduce \textbf{Detail Guidance Attack (DGA)}, a framework that uses an auxiliary LLM to construct detailed requests and interacts with the victim model in a single turn. Across 11 victim models and three datasets, the complete DGA pipeline achieves high attack success rates under our automated judging criterion, including rates above 95\% in several evaluated settings. We also evaluate a DGA-aware filter and conduct a user study on everyday requests with ambiguous or dual-use intent. The survey documents differing expectations about whether models should respond; the usability costs of the filter remain to be measured.
papers.authors: Wenzhuo Xu, Zonghao Ying, Deyue Zhang, Dongdong Yang, Xiangzheng Zhang, Quanchen Zou

papers.title: Optimized Solving Strategy and Two-Step Estimator for LWE with Hints
papers.abstract: Side-channel hints can reduce the cost of solving the Learning with Errors (LWE) problem. We optimize a two-step strategy for LWE with hints that uses BKZ reduction followed by final lattice sieving. Given a lattice constructed from the hints and a specified pair of reduction and sieving algorithms, the strategy jointly selects BKZ block sizes, tour counts, and a final sieving configuration. We also introduce a two-step estimator that predicts the reduced-basis profile and estimates the probability of secret recovery. We combine these estimates with cost models to select a strategy that meets the success-probability and resource constraints. Experiments show that our strategy significantly outperforms the methods of Cao et al. (CRYPTO 2025) and May and Nowakowski (ASIACRYPT 2023). For example, using BLASterBKZ for lattice reduction and the BGJ sieve for final sieving, our strategy recovers the secret for a CRYSTALS-KYBER 512 instance with 190 perfect hints in 7 minutes, compared with 1.6 hours reported by Cao et al. and 7.4 hours reported by May and Nowakowski. With 64 threads, our strategy recovers the secret with 170 perfect hints in 82 minutes. These results highlight the importance of accounting for side-channel leakage when assessing lattice-based cryptographic schemes.
papers.authors: Hanbin Yang, Jinzheng Cao, Risheng Yin, Qingfeng Cheng

papers.title: Toward Eﬃcient Post-Quantum Bitcoin Bridges
papers.abstract: BitVM-style protocols verify succinct proofs on Bitcoin by garbling a proof veriﬁer oﬀ-chain. What reaches the chain in a dispute is the proof itself: its bits under one-time keys, the scripts that authenticate them and the signatures that bind them to transactions. Existing designs garble elliptic-curve succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge (SNARK) veriﬁers, which a quantum adversary breaks. Our goal is a post-quantum alternative: a hash-based scalable transparent argument of knowledge (STARK) veriﬁer, garbled and fed with hash-based one-time keys, with no number-theoretic assumption anywhere in the veriﬁer; its price is a far larger proof, and this paper measures and reduces that on-chain data. We compile the complete veriﬁer for WHIR-based STARK proofs from Ziren into a Boolean circuit using free-XOR gadgets for binary-tower arithmetic and Blake3. Our implementation uses Ziren’s binary-ﬁeld proof stage and narrow recursion. For an Ethereum block proved through four recursion levels, the ﬁnal recursive WHIR-proof veriﬁer has 175.4M non-free gates and 520,832 input bits, corresponding to 2.81 GB of garbled tables, and publishing that input with translated Winternitz keys takes 3.93 million virtual bytes (MvB), in 41 standard transactions. The costs are coupled: on-chain cost grows linearly with the input bits, oﬀ-chain storage with the gate count, and proving time exponentially with the grinding that shortens the input. The WHIR schedule, the Merkle cap depth and the input encoding trade these costs against one another, and a model of proof size and proving time selects the setting, a step toward practical post-quantum Bitcoin bridges.
papers.authors: Stephen Duan, Vanhger Pham, Blake Hou, Ethan Zhu, Jingping Yin

papers.title: Triads below the ISA: Optimizing Cryptographic Software in CPU Microcode
papers.abstract: Cryptographic software is typically optimized for the instruction set architecture exposed by the processor. Modern processors, however, contain deeper execution layers with computational capabilities and constraints that differ from those of the instruction set architecture (ISA). This work explores the programmable microcode layer in x86 as an implementation target. We characterize the microcode domain as a distinct target architecture for cryptographic computation and adapt implementations to the state, operations, invocation interface, capacity, and scheduling resources it exposes. We instantiate this methodology on Intel Goldmont with Keccak f [1600] and X25519, two case studies with substantially different computational structures. Our Keccak implementation reduces permutation latency by 7.36% relative to the fastest native implementation in our comparison, with the improvement remaining visible in incomplete SHA3-256 computations. For X25519, our microcode multiplication and squaring kernels free the multiplier from fixed operand registers and restrictive carry-flag semantics, outperforming the native implementations we evaluate. The resulting complete X25519 implementation requires 7.3% fewer cycles than s2n-bignum and 9.8% fewer cycles than OpenSSL. Together, these results demonstrate that looking below the ISA exposes a distinct design space for cryptographic implementation and provide a systematic methodology for exploring it.
papers.authors: Sabrina Manickam, Rowan Fimmano, Peter Schwabe, Yuval Yarom

papers.title: Encrypted Authorship Attribution for Fraud Detection
papers.abstract: Authorship attribution techniques are routinely used to re- late anonymous or disputed texts to known authors through characteris- tic writing styles. Within the financial sector, such techniques may sup- port investigations of phishing campaigns, impersonation attempts, in- vestment scams, or other forms of fraud. More concretely, these methods can be leveraged to determine whether newly observed communications are linked to previously identified actors. In practice, however, both the communications under investigation and the intelligence databases used for attribution may contain sensitive information that cannot be shared across organizational boundaries. In this work, we investigate the privacy-preserving evaluation of sty- lometric authorship attribution through fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). We focus on Burrows’ Delta, a widely studied authorship attribu- tion method based on token frequency statistics and z-score comparisons. We present a homomorphic implementation of Burrows’ Delta, describe a motivating fraud-analysis scenario together with its threat model and trust assumptions, and then analyze the resulting computational com- plexity. Finally, we evaluate the practicality of the proposed approach us- ing the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme and show that the com- plete pipeline can be executed without bootstrapping while maintaining high numerical accuracy. Our results demonstrate that stylometric au- thorship attribution constitutes a realistic target for privacy-preserving outsourced analytics and illustrate how homomorphic encryption can support confidential fraud investigations.
papers.authors: Zita Baronnet, Leonard Schild

papers.title: On the Security of the Cubic UOV Variant CML
papers.abstract: CML is a cubic multivariate signature scheme proposed over $\mathbb{F}_q$ with $q = 2^8$. Earlier cubic Oil--Vinegar variants such as CUOV and CSSv were broken by differential and high-rank attacks. CML adds an $\ell$-invertible cycle system and a secret position-hiding map to hide the cubic positions. We show that the cubic homogeneous parts of the public key span a space of dimension at most two, so a publicly derived output combination has degree at most two. After restriction to the oil-direction space, the polar matrices of the publicly derived quadratic components span rank-two matrices associated with the edges of a path. This structure yields a procedure for recovering an equivalent key. Our implementation recovered an equivalent key in under 5~minutes for each tested parameter set, including the set targeting 256-bit security.
papers.authors: Manit Gupta

papers.title: Security Analysis of Anonymous Authentication in Apple's Private Cloud Compute
papers.abstract: Apple's Private Cloud Compute (PCC) offloads on-device computation, such as large language-model prompts, to the cloud while seeking to preserve the privacy users expect from local processing. At its core lies a custom authentication protocol that must reconcile three competing goals: restricting access to registered users within a rate limit, doing so without revealing user identities or linking their requests, and nonetheless retaining the ability to hold misbehaving users accountable. Apple's protocol combines blind RSA signatures in a hierarchical issuance with a salted-hash binding trick, but ships without any formal statement -- let alone proof -- of the guarantees it is meant to provide. In this work we close this gap by abstracting the desired authentication protocol as PORTA -- pseudonymously openable, rate-limited tokens for anonymous authentication. We formally define the desired privacy, security, and abuse-mitigation properties such a protocol should satisfy, including a new binding notion specific to the protocol's two-step issuance. We then cast Apple's protocol in this model and show that it achieves the rate-limiting goal and, with a small modification, all privacy goals. Its abuse-mitigation mechanism, which is not yet active in the deployed system, would however not provide the desired accountability guarantees even once enabled. Finally, we present an alternative construction based on anonymous credentials that provably achieves all properties and verifies the binding of tokens already at the gateway, so that a user's pseudonym is only revealed in case of abuse.
papers.authors: Callista Gratz, Anja Lehmann, Andrey Sidorenko

papers.title: Anamorphic NIZK: Definition, Construction and More
papers.abstract: Anamorphic encryption enables covert communication despite disclosure of ordinary decryption keys~\cite{PersianoPY22}. Work on anamorphic signatures extends this capability to settings permitting only authentication and shows that Fiat-Shamir preserves anamorphism~\cite{kutylowski2023anamorphicSignatures,fiat1986prove}. However, this result assumes an already anamorphic protocol and does not by itself ensure witness privacy against the recipient, motivating anamorphism directly in non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs (NIZKs). We introduce anamorphic NIZK (ANIZK), in which publicly verifiable proofs carry covert messages recoverable with a double key. The framework formalizes anamorphic security, strong robustness, and recipient anamorphic zero knowledge and simulation extractability. A generic construction in the random oracle model combines suitable Sigma protocols with authenticated encryption with associated data through a salted Fiat-Shamir transform. Applying ANIZK within the Naor-Yung paradigm \cite{NaorYung90} yields recipient anamorphic encryption satisfying STE-xCCA1, SIND-aCCA1, and SIND-nCCA security under the notions of~\cite{choi2026unified}. Finally, an asymmetric variant of ANIZK, termed ASY-ANIZK, combines a labeled NIZK with public-key encryption satisfying ciphertext pseudorandomness and random ciphertext rejection. It separates public embedding from secret recovery and achieves weak robustness, as public embedding precludes strong robustness.
papers.authors: Wenhui Kong, Gongxian Zeng, Zhengan Huang

papers.title: Tightly Secure and Modular Post-Quantum TLS Handshakes
papers.abstract: In the post-quantum (PQ) migration of the TLS~1.3 handshake, the classical Diffie--Hellman key exchange is replaced with a post-quantum key encapsulation mechanism (KEM). Furthermore, KEMTLS builds upon PQ TLS~1.3 by replacing signature-based authentication with KEM-based authentication. However, all existing analyses of PQ TLS~1.3 and KEMTLS incur at least quadratic reduction losses in the number of sessions, and achieving a tightly secure construction remains an open problem. To address this gap, we present the first unified, tight, and modular reduction framework for PQ TLS~1.3 in the standard model and KEMTLS in the random oracle model (ROM). Our framework tightly reduces the security of these protocols to the security of three core components: (i) the MUC-IND-1RCCA or MUC-IND-1CCA security of the underlying ephemeral KEM, (ii) the MU-(dual)-PRF security of HKDF (for PQ~TLS~1.3), and (iii) the MU-EUF-CMA$^c$ security of the signature scheme (for PQ TLS~1.3) or the MUC-OW-ChCCA$^*$ security of the static KEM (for KEMTLS). Furthermore, we establish the first concrete MU-(dual)-PRF bounds for HMAC and HKDF in the quantum-accessible random oracle model (QROM). Instantiating this framework with tightly secure LWE-based KEM and signature schemes yields the first (almost) tightly secure constructions of PQ TLS~1.3 and KEMTLS under the LWE assumption. Moreover, our framework demonstrates that the weaker IND-1RCCA security notion for the ephemeral KEM already suffices to achieve security for both PQ TLS~1.3 and KEMTLS, thereby enabling simpler instantiations.
papers.authors: Biming Zhou, Jinrong Chen, Haodong Jiang, Rongmao Chen, Yunlei Zhao

papers.title: SEC: One-Share Everywhere-Short Secret Sharing from Lossless Expanders
papers.abstract: We introduce SEC, an expander-code-based ramp secret sharing scheme over $\mathbb{Z}$-modules, particularly suitable for lattice-based distributed cryptography. It is everywhere-short: bounded secret coefficients yield bounded share coefficients, and the integer reconstruction vectors have bounded entries. Moreover, each participant receives exactly one share, regardless of the number of parties and the privacy and reconstruction thresholds. This improves on prior schemes with bounded share coefficients and bounded entries in the integer reconstruction vectors, in which the number of sub-shares or shares per participant grows either with the number of parties and the threshold or with the security parameter. The construction rests on a coding-theoretic observation: in the bi-adjacency matrix of a lossless bipartite expander, unique-neighbor peeling completes every sufficiently small set of columns to a square unimodular submatrix. We prove correctness, everywhere-shortness, and linearity, and give a publicly computable entrywise bound on the reconstruction vector our algorithm returns for each authorized set. For privacy, we introduce hard-core local leakage resilience, which strengthens the leakage-resilience notion of Nielsen and Simkin (EUROCRYPT 2020) to protect a hard-core function of the secret, and we prove that SEC satisfies it against correlated multi-query local leakage under the MatrixHint-MLWE problem, which admits a reduction from the standard MLWE problem. For $n=60$ participants and security parameter $κ=128$, SEC achieves privacy threshold 6 against $2^{64}$ leakage queries and empirical reconstruction threshold 46. The ideal entropy-coded secret and share sizes are about 3.5 KiB and 6.4 KiB, respectively.
papers.authors: Muhammad Arzaki, Muhammed F. Esgin, Amin Sakzad, Ron Steinfeld

papers.title: BMRaccoon: Blind Multi-Signatures from Lattices
papers.abstract: Blind multi-signatures (BMS) allow a user to obtain a compact signature on a hidden message through the joint participation of multiple signers, providing a basis for decentralized issuance of anonymous tokens.We present BMRaccoon, the first lattice-based post-quantum BMS construction, with a two-round signing protocol secure under concurrent sessions and signatures syntactically compatible with Raccoon under the sum of the signers' verification keys. As a building block, we introduce MRaccoon, the first Raccoon-based multi-signature and prove its strong unforgeability under the Algebraic One-More MISIS (AOM-MISIS) and MSIS assumptions in the random oracle and and knowledge-of-secret-key (KOSK) model. Our modular security analysis establishes one-more unforgeability of BMRaccoon via a straight-line reduction to the strong unforgeability of MRaccoon, modelling the user's blinding contribution as an auxiliary signer with a zero verification key. We additionally prove blindness against malicious, colluding signers. For up to $q_s = 2^{32}$ signing sessions and $n = 32$ signers, our concrete instantiation yields signatures of approximately $67$ KB and verification keys of approximately $15$ KB.
papers.authors: Keerthi Aiswarya Varshini, Kanchan Bisht, Palkesh Jain, Maria Francis, R. Kabaleeshwaran

papers.title: A Single-Trace Side-Channel Attack on the KpqC Digital Signature Scheme AIMer v3
papers.abstract: The Korean Post-Quantum Cryptography (KpqC) competition selected AIMer, a post-quantum digital signature scheme based on the MPC-in-the-Head paradigm, as one of its final algorithms in 2025. However, detailed side-channel analysis (SCA) of AIMer remains limited, particularly for its latest version, AIMer v3.
